0.title: Last Words: The Final Letter of the Apostle Paul
0.overview:
The message. Second Timothy is a last will and testament, a soldier’s final dispatch from the front and a father’s farewell to his son, all at once. Paul is in chains in Rome and expects to die soon: “the time of my departure has come” (4:6). Before he goes he hands on to Timothy the one thing that matters most, the gospel of Jesus Christ, crucified and risen. Guard it, suffer for it if you must, pass it on, preach it. The letter is addressed to a minister, but it speaks to every Christian who has been given something precious to hold in a world that does not want it.

Background: the writer. The letter names Paul as its author (1:1), and it is a prisoner’s letter: he is “bound with chains as a criminal” (2:9), and Onesiphorus had to search Rome to find him (1:17). Acts ends with Paul under house arrest, preaching freely (Acts 28:30–31). Here things are harsher: he has already had a “first defense” at which no one stood by him (4:16), he does not expect to be released, and most of his friends have gone. The early church believed Paul was freed after Acts, travelled again and was arrested a second time; this letter fits that last imprisonment. A later tradition places him in the Mamertine Prison below the Capitoline Hill, where prisoners awaited execution. It was probably written about AD 64–67, shortly before he died.

Rome under Nero. The emperor was Nero. After the great fire of Rome in AD 64 he blamed the Christians, and many were put to death in cruel ways. To be known as a Christian, or as the friend of a Christian prisoner, was now dangerous. That lies behind the letter’s repeated call not to be ashamed (1:8, 12, 16) and its plain warning, “all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (3:12). The early church remembered that Paul was executed in Rome under Nero, by tradition beheaded, as a Roman citizen could be.

The first reader. Timothy probably came from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father (Acts 16:1–3). His grandmother Lois and mother Eunice had taught him the Scriptures “from childhood” (1:5; 3:15). Paul took him on his travels as a young man and sent him on hard errands. He was probably still in Ephesus, where Paul had left him to deal with false teachers (1 Timothy 1:3; compare 2 Timothy 1:18; 4:19). He seems to have been young for his task and inclined to timidity (1:6–7; compare 1 Corinthians 16:10–11), and the pressure to tone the gospel down for the sake of peace was real. Some in the church, Hymenaeus and Philetus among them, were teaching “that the resurrection has already happened” (2:17–18).

Paul the man. Few of Paul’s letters let us see him so closely. He remembers Timothy’s tears and longs to see him (1:4). He is warmed by the courage of Onesiphorus, who “was not ashamed of my chains” (1:16), and stung by the harm done by Alexander the coppersmith (4:14). “All who are in Asia turned away from me” (1:15); Demas, “in love with this present world”, has deserted him; “Luke alone is with me” (4:10–11). Winter is coming, and he asks for the cloak he left at Troas, and for his books and parchments (4:13, 21): he is still reading and studying to the end. He asks for Mark, the man he once refused to take with him (Acts 15:37–39), because “he is very useful to me for ministry” (4:11). The great apostle is cold, lonely and facing death, yet the letter is not a cry of despair but an act of faith.

Did Paul really write it? Many modern scholars think the three Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy and Titus) were written after Paul’s death by a follower using his name, pointing to their vocabulary and style, their concern for church order, and travels that do not fit into Acts; some think this letter at least contains genuine notes of Paul’s. But it names Paul as its author, the early church received it as his, and its personal details, a cloak at Troas, a sick colleague left at Miletus (4:20), are hard to explain as invention. Differences of style suit an older apostle writing to a trusted co-worker on new subjects, perhaps through a secretary, and the travels fit a release after Acts. A letter claiming to be Paul’s that was not would be a forgery, and the church of that day rejected such letters. The more likely conclusion, and the view of this commentary, is that Paul wrote it.

How the letter makes its case. Chapter 1 calls Timothy not to be ashamed: to “fan into flame the gift of God” (1:6), to share in suffering for a gospel that rests on God’s grace given “before the ages began” (1:9), and to “guard the good deposit” (1:14). Chapter 2 tells him to be strong in grace and pass the gospel on to “faithful men, who will be able to teach others also” (2:2): four generations in one verse. He is to endure like a soldier, an athlete and a farmer, to handle the word of truth rightly, and to correct opponents with gentleness as the Lord’s servant. Chapter 3 warns of the “times of difficulty” of the last days (3:1), which this commentary takes to mean the whole age between Christ’s comings, and sends Timothy back to what he learned and to the Scriptures, which are “breathed out by God” and make the man of God “complete, equipped for every good work” (3:16–17). Chapter 4 brings the solemn charge, “preach the word” (4:2), and then Paul’s farewell: “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (4:7), with the last news, requests and greetings.

Where it leads: to Christ. At the centre of the letter stands one command: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David” (2:8). He is the Saviour “who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel” (1:10), the one Paul has trusted: “I know whom I have believed” (1:12). He is the coming Judge “of the living and the dead” (4:1), who will give the crown of righteousness to Paul “and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing” (4:8). When every friend failed at the first defense, “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (4:17). Paul can be bound, but “the word of God is not bound!” (2:9). Faith in this risen Lord is the one thing that has not been shaken.

For us. What Paul entrusted to Timothy is the same treasure entrusted to every generation of the church. We are not its owners but its stewards: to guard it, to live by the Scriptures that carry it, to suffer for it without shame, and to hand it on to others who will hand it on again. The letter does not promise that faithfulness will be popular; it promises that the Lord will stand by his servants and bring them safely into his heavenly kingdom (4:18). Paul’s life proves the claim. The question it leaves with each of us is whether, at the end, we too will have kept the faith.

1.title: Guard the Deposit: Courage, the Gospel, and Faithful Examples
1.overview:
Where we are. This is the opening of Paul’s last letter, written from a Roman prison as he expects to die (4:6). After the greeting (vv. 1–2) and his thanks for Timothy (vv. 3–5), he goes straight to the charge that governs the whole letter.

The message. Do not be ashamed of the gospel, or of the people who suffer for it, because the God who gave it is stronger than everything that threatens it. He saved us by a grace given in Christ before time began, and Christ has abolished death; so stir up the gift, share in the suffering by God’s power, and guard the treasure entrusted to you, knowing that the Lord guards what you have entrusted to him.

Why it was said. Timothy was young for his task and inclined to timidity, and under Nero to be linked with a chained prisoner on a capital charge was dangerous (see the introduction). Almost everyone in Asia had already decided it was not worth the risk (v. 15). Paul needed to know that the gospel would outlive him in safe hands.

How the chapter makes its case. The word “ashamed” comes three times (vv. 8, 12, 16) and holds the chapter together. Paul first reminds Timothy of what he already has: a sincere faith handed down from Lois and Eunice (vv. 3–5) and a gift of God, with a Spirit of power, love and self-control (vv. 6–7). He then gives the charge (v. 8) and its ground, one of the richest summaries of the gospel in the New Testament (vv. 9–10). He sets his own example beside it: he suffers, but is not ashamed, because he knows whom he has believed (vv. 11–12). Two deposits face each other: what Paul has entrusted to the Lord, and what the Lord has entrusted to Timothy, to be guarded by the Holy Spirit (vv. 12–14). Last come two examples, the many who turned away and the one man, Onesiphorus, who searched Rome until he found Paul (vv. 15–18).

Where it leads. Everything rests on Christ Jesus. Grace was given in him before the ages; he appeared, abolished death and brought life and immortality to light; he is the One Paul knows and trusts, who keeps what is entrusted to him until that day. He was not ashamed to bear our shame and our chains, and he is the Judge before whom no act of faithful love will be forgotten.

For us. Every believer is tempted to keep quiet about Christ, or to keep a safe distance from Christians who have become unpopular. This chapter does not answer with a lecture on bravery but with the gospel: you have been saved, death is beaten, and your life is in safe hands. Then it asks whether you will be a Phygelus or an Onesiphorus.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul writes as Christ’s appointed messenger of life to the son he loves. The opening sentence already holds the letter’s surprise: a man about to be executed calls himself an apostle “according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus” (v. 1), and he greets Timothy not as a colleague to be instructed but as his dearly loved child, wishing him grace, mercy and peace from the Father and the Son (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology:
A Personal Letter, Not a Church Order

There is no thanksgiving for a congregation because none is in view: this is an old man writing to a younger one while there is still time, and ‘mercy’ appears in the greeting as it does only in the letters to Timothy.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul calls himself the Lord's prisoner, not Rome's (v.8; cf. Eph 3:1).

Now: ‘The promise of the life’ is the letter's whole argument in its first sentence (see the note on vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God according to the promise of the life that is in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes as an apostle sent to announce the promise of life in Christ, to a son he dearly loves. A man about to be executed opens his last letter by speaking of life, and with tenderness.

An apostle by the will of God. Paul stands where he always has (1 Corinthians 1:1; Galatians 1:1). Whatever a Roman court decides about him, his appointment came from somewhere no court can reach. The man in chains is still the King’s envoy.

The promise of the life. Here is the first surprise of the letter: a man facing execution names his commission in terms of life. The promise is life found only in union with Christ (John 11:25–26; 1 John 5:11–12): to know the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom he sent (John 17:3). It begins the moment a person is joined to Christ, and death stops the breathing but not the knowing. Rome can end Paul’s breathing. It cannot touch this life, because it is in Christ Jesus, and Christ Jesus has already been raised from the dead.

My beloved child. In the first letter Timothy was “my true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2), genuine as against the counterfeits in Ephesus. Here he is “my beloved child” (agapētō): the contrast with opponents has dropped away, and these are a dying father’s words.

Grace, mercy, and peace. The triple blessing of 1 Timothy 1:2: grace for the undeserving, mercy for the suffering, peace for the troubled. Mercy is needed even more now, for Timothy is about to be asked to come to a man most have abandoned, and to take up a trust that has cost its last holder everything. Paul names Jesus alongside the Father as the one source of these gifts, because Jesus is God; and the Father of mercies sends them to a lonely young pastor through the hand of a condemned man.

The setting. This imprisonment is harsher than the house arrest of Acts 28: Paul is chained, hard to find and largely deserted, and expects execution (see the introduction).

In everyday life. When you speak to someone younger in the faith, begin as Paul does, not with instructions but with love. Correction lands differently on someone who has first been told he is beloved.

Why does Paul still call himself an apostle, and are there apostles today? Paul names his office because this letter carries Christ’s authority, not merely an old friend’s advice. An apostle in this sense was personally commissioned by the risen Christ as a witness of his resurrection (1 Corinthians 9:1; 15:8), sent to lay the church’s foundation (Ephesians 2:20), and foundations are laid once. So Paul hands the work on not to new apostles but to Timothy and to faithful men who will teach others (2:2). Missionaries and church planters are sometimes loosely called apostolic, but no one now carries Paul’s authority. We hear the apostles by reading what they wrote, which is why this letter is Scripture and not merely a moving keepsake.
verseByVerse.note: Paul’s last surviving letter, written from prison in Rome as he expected to die, probably in the mid 60s AD under Nero. Timothy was probably still in Ephesus.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–14 — Fan Into Flame, and Guard the Deposit
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Do not be ashamed of the gospel, because the God who gave it is greater than all that threatens it. Paul begins with what Timothy already has: a sincere faith (vv. 3–5) and a gift and Spirit from God (vv. 6–7). Then comes the charge to share in suffering (v. 8), grounded in God’s grace given before the ages and in Christ’s victory over death (vv. 9–10). Paul’s own example follows (vv. 11–12), and the section ends where it is heading: guard the good deposit, by the Holy Spirit who lives in you (vv. 13–14).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Deposits, Running Opposite Ways

Paul has entrusted his deposit to God (v.12); God has entrusted a deposit to Timothy (v.14); see “The architecture of the chapter” in the note on vv. 13–14. And behind both stands the grace given in Christ before the ages began, by the Saviour who abolished death (vv.9–10).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The faith came to Timothy through his grandmother and mother (Acts 16:1), long before any laying on of hands (see the note on v. 5).

Now: To a timid man Paul names what he has been given (see the note on vv. 6–7).

verseByVerse.quote: I thank God whom I serve, as did my ancestors, with a clear conscience, as I remember you constantly in my prayers night and day. As I remember your tears, I long to see you, that I may be filled with joy.
verseByVerse.commentary:
From his cell Paul thanks God for Timothy, prays for him night and day, and longs to see him. He serves the God of his forefathers with a clean conscience, and he is not too heroic to need a friend.

As did my ancestors. Paul’s word for serving (latreuō) is the word for worship at the tabernacle and temple. His Jewish inheritance was no false start: he worships the God of Abraham, Moses and David, whom his forefathers (progonōn) served (Acts 24:14; 26:6–7). The gospel was not a change of God but the arrival of what that God had promised.

A clear conscience. Clear means clean (kathara): not sinlessness but integrity, a conscience that does not accuse him of hypocrisy in his ministry (Acts 23:1; 24:16). The first letter made conscience a recurring test (1 Timothy 1:5, 19); at the end of his life, with nothing left unsettled, Paul quietly claims what he required of others.

Night and day. “Constantly” (adialeiptōs) means without ceasing. In a cell where day and night blur together, an old man may well have prayed for his friend at three in the morning. His world has shrunk to a few square yards, and his prayers still reach Ephesus.

Your tears. Somewhere there had been a parting, and Timothy had wept, as the Ephesian elders had at Miletus (Acts 20:37). Paul does not call the tears weakness; the Lord Jesus wept at a grave he was about to empty (John 11:35), and God stores his people’s tears (Psalm 56:8).

I long to see you. “Long” (epipotheō) is to yearn. Paul wants the visit not for Timothy’s comfort but for his own joy: the man facing execution with composure says openly that there is a joy he lacks, and that a visit from this young man would supply it. Contentment in Paul never meant needing nobody.

Priestly service with a cleansed conscience. Paul puts the temple word and the clean conscience in one sentence, and Hebrews shows why. The sacrifices of his ancestors could not perfect the worshipper’s conscience, but the blood of Christ purifies our conscience from dead works to serve the living God (Hebrews 9:9, 14), with Paul’s verb here. The forefathers’ worship was not cancelled when Christ came but completed, for the sacrifice their altars pointed to has been offered once for all (Hebrews 10:10).

In everyday life. Sleepless hours, waiting rooms and long drives are good places for prayer. And a short message telling someone plainly that you miss them costs little and can mean a great deal.

How can my conscience be clear when I know what I have done? In the same way Paul’s was. He had been a blasphemer and a persecutor (1 Timothy 1:13), and his conscience was clean not because he had forgotten but because the blood of Christ had answered it (Hebrews 9:14; 10:22). A clear conscience is not a clean record but nothing hidden between you and God: known sins confessed, and where possible put right with those you wronged. If it accuses you of something already confessed, answer it with the cross, not more penance. If it accuses you of something never dealt with, listen, and deal with it today.

Is it wrong for a Christian to feel lonely or to need people? No. Paul, filled with the Spirit and certain of heaven, longs to see a friend. God said, “It is not good that the man should be alone” (Genesis 2:18), and Jesus wanted his friends near him in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:38). Needing people is part of bearing the image of a God who is himself a fellowship of love; the danger is needing them in place of God. Paul has both: Christ stands by him when everyone else has gone (4:17), and still he asks Timothy to come.

verseByVerse.quote: I am reminded of your sincere faith, a faith that dwelt first in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice and now, I am sure, dwells in you as well.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy’s faith is real, and it came to him through the quiet teaching of his grandmother and his mother. Paul reminds a timid young man that what he has is genuine.

Your sincere faith. “Sincere” (anypokritos) means without hypocrisy, with no actor’s mask (1 Timothy 1:5). Whatever Timothy’s timidity, Paul has no doubt his faith is genuine: a frightened believer and a false believer are very different things. And “I am sure” (pepeismai) is offered to a man who evidently needed to hear it. Some people need someone else to tell them that what they have is real.

Lois and Eunice. Three generations, named. Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek (Acts 16:1), so the faith came down the female line, probably from Paul’s first visit to Lystra (Acts 14:6–7). “Dwelt” (enōkēsen) means made its home: faith was no visitor in that house. And notice how it travelled. Paul has spent two letters on overseers, elders and public teaching, but the man he entrusts everything to was formed by two women teaching a child the sacred writings at home (3:15). Nobody laid hands on Lois. God takes the hidden faithfulness of people no one has heard of and builds his church on it.

Faith waiting for its name. Lois and Eunice were very likely devout Jewish women whose trust in God’s promises had a direction before it had a name: the faith of Abraham, who rejoiced that he would see Christ’s day (John 8:56). When Paul came to Lystra preaching Jesus crucified and risen, that faith found the one it had been waiting for. Sincere faith is not sincerity about anything at all; it is real trust, resting on Christ.

In everyday life. Thank God, by name, for those who taught you the faith, and if they are living, tell them.

My children or grandchildren do not believe. What does this verse say to me? That your teaching is not wasted, and it is not the last word. Lois and Eunice could not give Timothy faith; only God could, and he used their teaching when the gospel came. You cannot convert your children either, and you were never asked to. You are asked to teach them, pray for them, live what you say before them and keep loving them, even if all they will now receive is your life and an occasional honest word. God has brought many prodigals home through seeds planted decades earlier. Leave the outcome with him; your peace rests on his faithfulness, not on their response.

I was not raised in a Christian home. Am I behind? No. Paul was converted as a grown man who had spent years attacking the church, and most of the first Christians had no Christian upbringing at all. God has no second-class children. A Christian home is a great mercy and a great responsibility, but not a head start in grace. And you can be a Lois: the faith that came to you first can dwell in your house and be handed on, and your children may one day thank God for the one who started it.

Where Christians differ: are children of believers automatically in the covenant? Paedobaptists (Christians who baptise the infants of believers) see verses like this as evidence that God’s covenant runs on through believing families, as it did in Israel, and so as support for infant baptism. This commentary’s view: The verse shows the great value of believing parents and grandparents who teach their children the Scriptures from infancy; God often works through families. But faith is not inherited; each person must come to faith personally (John 1:12–13), as Timothy did. Scripture does not record his baptism, but its pattern is that those who believe are then baptised (Acts 2:41; 8:12): baptism belongs to those who profess faith. This is held charitably toward our paedobaptist brothers, who equally insist that each child must come to personal faith.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy’s father was a Greek; his faith came through his mother’s side.

verseByVerse.quote: For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because his faith is real, Timothy must stir his gift back into flame, for the Spirit God gives makes his servants bold, loving and clear-headed, not cowardly. Paul tells a frightened man what he has been given, not what he must work up in himself.

Fan into flame. “For this reason” looks back to verse 5: real faith can still burn low. The verb (anazōpyreō) means to stir a fire back into blaze, and implies embers, not ashes: the gift has not gone out; it needs air. Paul does not rebuke a man whose fire has dimmed under long pressure; he tells him to stir it up. The “gift” (charisma) is his gift for ministry (1 Timothy 4:14), and a gift is kept bright by use.

The laying on of my hands. The gift came when the elders laid hands on him (1 Timothy 4:14), and Paul was among them. The old man about to die wants Timothy to remember whose hands were on his head.

A spirit not of fear. This is why the fire had dimmed. The word is not the ordinary term for fear but deilia: cowardice, the shrinking that stops a man doing what he knows he should, and Timothy seems to have been naturally timid (1 Corinthians 16:10). God gave us his Spirit, and he is not a Spirit of cowardice (on “spirit”, see the box below).

Power and love and self-control. Against timidity, three gifts, and each answers something. Power (dynamis), because the task is beyond him, and it always was (Acts 1:8). Love (agapē), because fear makes a man self-protective, and love is the only thing that reliably gets him outside himself (1 John 4:18). And self-control (sōphronismos), a sound mind, because a frightened man’s estimate of his situation is seldom accurate.

The Spirit who rested on Christ. These three gifts were seen first in Jesus, on whom the Spirit of counsel and might rested (Isaiah 11:2): he returned from the wilderness in the power of the Spirit (Luke 4:14), loved his own to the end (John 13:1), and stood before Pilate with a clear head and few words. The Spirit given to Timothy is the Spirit who filled Jesus, poured out by the exalted Christ (Acts 2:33). Timothy is not told to become a different man by effort. God does not hand his frightened servants a lecture on bravery; he gives them himself, and he does not quench a smouldering wick (Isaiah 42:3) but breathes on it until it burns.

In everyday life. What has fear stopped you doing for Christ: the conversation you keep postponing, the truth you softened? Ask the Spirit for power, love and a clear head, and take one step this week while you are still afraid. Courage is rarely the absence of the feeling; it is obedience with the feeling still there.

Is fear itself a sin? Paul is speaking of the cowardice that shrinks back from duty and from suffering for Christ, not of every feeling of fear. Many faithful believers feel afraid, and some suffer from anxiety that has bodily causes; that is not condemned here. The Spirit gives power, love and self-control to act faithfully even when we are afraid.

What is my gift, and how do I fan it into flame? Every believer has some gift from the Spirit for the good of others (1 Peter 4:10–11; Romans 12:6–8). You usually find it not by introspection but by serving the needs in front of you and listening when mature believers say people are helped when you do that. Then keep it burning: use it regularly, feed it with Scripture and prayer, keep away from what smothers it (unconfessed sin, bitterness, sheer busyness), and stay close to others who stir you up. A gift left unused cools; a gift used in love grows.

Does the laying on of hands pass on spiritual power today? Not as the apostles’ hands did. The apostles had a unique foundational role as witnesses of the risen Christ (Ephesians 2:20), and this commentary holds that the sign gifts that accompanied them ceased with that role (cessationism), because Scripture ties those signs to the apostles’ founding witness (2 Corinthians 12:12; Hebrews 2:3–4). Many faithful Christians, including Pentecostal and charismatic believers, hold that such gifts continue today, and they too insist that every gift comes from God, not from human hands. Churches rightly lay hands on those set apart as elders or missionaries, as a public sign of recognition and prayer (Acts 13:3), but no one needs a special person to touch them before the Spirit can work in them.

Uncertain wording. Two phrases in verse 7 are not certain. “A spirit” may mean the Holy Spirit himself, as in verse 14 and Romans 8:15, or the disposition God gives, a frame of mind. Since God “gave” it, and power and love are the Spirit’s gifts, the Holy Spirit is most likely, and the two meanings meet: the Spirit produces the disposition. And sōphronismos occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It can mean self-control, a sound mind, or the discipline that brings others to their senses; most likely it is the steady, sober judgment that fear distorts.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must not be ashamed of the message about Jesus or of Paul in chains, but must share his suffering for the gospel, relying on God’s power. This is the charge at the heart of the chapter.

Do not be ashamed. “Ashamed” (epaischynthēs) governs this chapter, coming three times (here, v. 12 and v. 16). The first thing Timothy might be ashamed of is the message itself: announcing a crucified provincial as Lord was folly to Gentiles (1 Corinthians 1:23), and under Nero it was dangerous. Jesus had warned against exactly this shame (Mark 8:38), and Paul had refused it all his life (Romans 1:16).

Nor of me his prisoner. Here is the real difficulty. Association with a man awaiting execution is dangerous and humiliating, and verse 15 will say that everyone in Asia has already turned away. And Paul calls himself not Nero’s prisoner but the Lord’s (Ephesians 3:1). The chain is Roman; the ownership is not.

Share in suffering. Endure hardship alongside: one verb (synkakopathēson), perhaps Paul’s own coinage. Paul is not asking Timothy to be brave in his own separate trouble but to come and take a share of this one. Suffering for the gospel is a fellowship, shared with Paul and, beneath that, with Christ (Philippians 3:10; 1 Peter 4:13).

By the power of God. Not by Timothy’s resolve. This is what the spirit of power (v. 7) is for: not a quality he must find in himself, but a supply to draw on (Colossians 1:11).

In the flow. The chapter now takes the two objects of shame in turn: the testimony about our Lord (vv. 9–10), and Paul the prisoner, who is not ashamed (vv. 11–12). Then verses 15–18 set those who were ashamed of him beside one man who was not.

Not ashamed of us. The Lord Jesus was not ashamed of us. He endured the cross, despising its shame (Hebrews 12:2), was numbered with criminals where the whole city could see, and is not ashamed to call us brothers (Hebrews 2:11). He was put to shame for us, and he will own us before his Father and the holy angels. What we share when we suffer for the gospel is not a lonely heroism but his own fellowship, and the power that carries us is the power that raised him.

What it does not mean. Not that we should seek suffering, or that all suffering is for the gospel; only that we must not dodge the suffering faithfulness brings. And where we have been ashamed of him, as every believer has, our standing with God does not rest on our courage. Christ confessed the truth without flinching, and his faithfulness is counted as ours (Romans 5:19). There is a way back, the way Peter took: confession and forgiveness (1 John 1:9).

In everyday life. Think of one fellow believer who is under pressure or out of favour, and stand next to them this week, publicly, in some small way.

What does being ashamed of the gospel look like today? Rarely like denying Christ outright. More often it is steering the conversation away when faith comes up at work, letting people assume you agree with them, or keeping a quiet distance from the Christian who has become unpopular for saying what you also believe. It can be preaching only the admired parts of the message and dropping sin, judgment and the cross. Shame is not the same as tact or wise timing; the test is whether, when it would cost you something, people would know that you belong to Jesus and his people. Underneath, shame is about whose approval we feel we cannot live without. The fear of man lays a snare, but the one who trusts in the Lord is safe (Proverbs 29:25); the cure is to be more taken with Christ’s welcome than with anyone else’s frown.

How do I draw on God’s power when I am afraid? Not by waiting until you feel strong; the power is usually given for the step, not before it. Remember that the God who asks this of you has already saved you (v. 9). Ask for help specifically and beforehand: “Lord, I have to speak tomorrow; give me courage and the right words” (compare Acts 4:29). Take the next small faithful step anyway, the honest answer, the quiet word about Christ, the visit to a friend in trouble, and expect strength as you go, as Paul found at his trial: “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (4:17). Ask another believer to pray, for this suffering is shared. And when you fail, go back to the One whose power is made perfect in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:9). He restored Peter after his denials, and Peter preached at Pentecost.

What if standing with someone costs me my job or my friends? Then you are in Timothy’s position, and Paul does not pretend the cost is small. He asks it anyway, because Christ is worth it and you will not bear it alone. Be wise; do not invite needless trouble, and obey lawful authorities where you can (Romans 13:1). But where the choice is between faithfulness and safety, Jesus has said what is at stake (Mark 8:38), and that no one who has left anything for his sake will fail to receive far more (Mark 10:29–30).

verseByVerse.quote: who saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began, and which now has been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Christ Jesus, who abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel,
verseByVerse.commentary:
God saved us and called us by his own grace, given in Christ before time began and now revealed in his coming, and Christ has put death out of action. This is why Timothy can face suffering: what they threaten him with has already been defeated.

Who saved us. Paul cannot mention God without describing him, and what follows is one of the densest statements of the gospel in the New Testament, perhaps already sung as a hymn. “Saved” (sōsantos) is past tense: it has been done. We are saved from the guilt of sin and God’s just anger against it (Romans 5:9), and from sin’s rule (Matthew 1:21). God did not lower his standard to save us; he rescued us from the punishment it rightly requires.

A holy calling. “Called” (kalesantos) is God’s effectual call, which brings his chosen ones to faith (Romans 8:30): not an invitation that may be refused but a summons that raises the dead, as Jesus called Lazarus out of the tomb. A holy calling is a calling to be holy (1 Thessalonians 4:7). God did not save you and leave you as you were; the call that brought you to faith now claims your body, your speech, your money and your time.

Not because of our works. Paul puts the “not” first, for emphasis. Salvation is not a reward for anything we have done, are doing, or will do (Ephesians 2:8–9; Titus 3:5), not even for foreseen works or foreseen faith. “Purpose” (prothesis) is a resolve set forth beforehand, and it is “his own”: the reason for salvation lies entirely in God. Nothing in us moved him; everything in him did. “Grace” (charis) is undeserved favour.

Before the ages began. Literally, before eternal times (pro chronōn aiōniōn), before time itself. Grace was not merely planned then: it was given, in Christ Jesus, before there was any world in which we could receive it. Before the first star was lit, before Adam was formed, the Father looked on his people in his Son and gave them grace. This is election: God chose his people in Christ before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4–5). Whatever else that means, nothing we have done since can be the reason.

Now has been manifested. Verse 10 brings it into history. “Appearing” (epiphaneia), used elsewhere of Christ’s second coming (1 Timothy 6:14), here means his first. What God planned in eternity he revealed in history, at Bethlehem, at Golgotha, at the empty tomb.

Who abolished death. Abolished means put out of action (katargēsantos), and it is past tense, written by a man on death row. Death has already been disarmed. Believers still die, but death can no longer hold them or separate them from God. Its sting, which is sin, has been removed (1 Corinthians 15:54–57), and those who all their lives were held in slavery by fear of it are set free (Hebrews 2:14–15).

Life and immortality. “Brought to light” (phōtisantos) is illuminated. “Immortality” (aphtharsia) is incorruptibility: the whole person beyond the reach of decay, not merely a surviving soul. Philosophers debated it, the secret religions sold it, tombstones denied it, the Old Testament glimpsed it (Job 19:25–27; Daniel 12:2). Paul says an event has lit it up. Christ came out of the grave, and the lights came on.

Why it is here. Paul writes all this to persuade a frightened young man to come and share his suffering. The argument is not “be brave” but: death has been abolished, so what exactly are they threatening you with? Doctrine is not a distraction from courage; it is its fuel.

In everyday life. When you are anxious about death, read verses 9 and 10 aloud, slowly, and listen to the tense of every verb: saved, called, gave, manifested, abolished, brought to light. All past. Your standing with God was given before you were born, and you cannot improve on a gift that old.

Isn’t hope beyond death just wishful thinking? The poet Philip Larkin, in “Aubade”, called religion “That vast moth-eaten musical brocade / Created to pretend we never die”. It is an honest charge and deserves an honest answer. Paul does not pretend. In a Roman cell, expecting the sword, he never calls death unreal or nothing to fear. He says it has been abolished, and points not to a feeling but to an appearing, something that happened in history and was seen (on the evidence, see the note on 1 Corinthians 15:12–19). It is our culture that pretends, keeping death out of sight and conversation and filling the time so full that we need never think about it. The gospel lets you look straight at death, because someone has gone through it and come out the other side. Wishful thinking invents a comfort to cover a fear; the Christian hope announces a defeat of death that is either true or false, and asks to be examined, not merely felt.

If God chose before time began, does it matter whether I preach or pray or believe? Yes, because the God who chose the end also chose the means. He saves through the gospel (v. 10), and people cannot believe in one of whom they have never heard (Romans 10:14). Election is why evangelism succeeds, not why it is unnecessary: Paul endures everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain salvation (2:10). And election is never a reason to wait: Jesus said, “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37).

Is it fair for God to choose some and not others? Fairness would give each of us what we have earned, and then no one would be saved, for God saved us not because of our works. No one is condemned because he was not chosen, but for the sins he freely loves (John 3:19). Election keeps no one away from Christ who wants him; it is the reason anyone wants him at all. Paul answered this objection with mercy: it depends not on human will or effort but on God, who has mercy (Romans 9:14–16). The wonder is not that some are passed over, but that any are saved.

How can I know that God chose me? Not by trying to read the secret decree, but by looking at Christ and at what God has done in you. If you trust in Christ, it is because God called you, and those he called he will glorify (Romans 8:30). The evidence is the marks of the holy calling: faith in Christ, love for him and his people, a desire to be holy, grief over sin (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5; 2 Peter 1:10). If you are unsure, do not begin with “Am I elect?” Begin with the invitation: come to Christ. Those who come find, afterwards, that they were sought before the ages.

Where Christians differ: is election based on foreseen faith? Arminian Christians (who hold that God’s saving grace can be resisted) teach that God chose those whom he foresaw would believe. They hold it out of a real concern for God’s fairness and for human responsibility, and many of them are earnest and fruitful believers. This commentary’s view: This verse rules it out: God saved us not because of our works but because of his own purpose and grace, given before time began. If election rested on foreseen faith, it would rest on something in us. Faith is the result of God’s choice, not its cause (Acts 13:48; Ephesians 2:8). This is unconditional election: God’s choice depended on no condition he saw in us. It is the strongest ground of assurance, for what God purposed before time he will not abandon. The questions of fairness and responsibility are real, and are taken up above.

verseByVerse.quote: for which I was appointed a preacher and apostle and teacher, which is why I suffer as I do. But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul suffers because of the commission Christ gave him, yet he is not ashamed, because he knows the One he trusts and is sure that he will keep safe what has been entrusted until the last day. The prisoner is not asking Timothy to bear something he is privately embarrassed about.

Preacher and apostle and teacher. The same three as 1 Timothy 2:7: herald (kēryx), who announces the King’s news; sent one (apostolos), who represents his sender; and teacher (didaskalos), who explains it. That is why he suffers: not for wrongdoing, but because of the appointment. And having told Timothy not to be ashamed of a prisoner, the prisoner says he is not ashamed either.

Whom I have believed. Here is the sentence that has held Christians steady for two thousand years. Paul does not say “what” but “whom”. His confidence at the end rests not on the soundness of his doctrine, though he has fought for it in every letter, but on a person he knows. “Have believed” (pepisteuka) is a perfect tense: I have trusted and I keep trusting. Doctrine matters enormously, but it is not what you lean on at the end; you lean on the one the doctrine is about.

He is able to guard. “Convinced” (pepeismai) is the word Paul used of Timothy’s faith (v. 5). “Guard” (phylaxai) is keep safe, as a sentry keeps a gate. “That day” is the day of Christ’s return and judgment (4:8). Paul looks straight past his own death to that day.

He has never lost one. He is able. The Christ who was entrusted with his people by the Father has never lost one of them (John 6:39), and he will not begin with you. He kept Paul to the end, through the sword on the road to Ostia, and he holds all who trust him in a hand from which no one can snatch them (John 10:28). He is the faithful keeper of souls, and he guards what we give him, until that day, and for ever.

In everyday life. List the things you cannot keep safe yourself: your children, your health, your future, your soul. Place them, one by one, in his hands in prayer, and when anxiety returns, remind yourself where you left them, and who is guarding them.

What if my faith feels weak? Then this verse is especially for you, because it does not put the weight on your grip. A weak hand holding a strong rope is safer than a strong hand holding a thread: faith saves not by its size but by its object, and a trembling faith unites you to Christ as surely as a bold one. Feed it by getting to know him better, in the Gospels and in prayer, since Paul’s confidence came from knowing whom. And when you cannot feel it at all, say what the father said to Jesus: “I believe; help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24). Jesus did not send him away.

Does this teach that a believer is kept to the end? Paul’s confidence is in God’s power to guard what has been entrusted to him. Arminian Christians hold that a believer must keep himself in the faith and may fail to. Believers must persevere, but it is God who keeps them (John 10:28; Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5), and that is why Paul can face death unashamed. This commentary holds that Reformed teaching, the perseverance of the saints, while honouring Arminian brothers who take Scripture’s warnings with equal seriousness.

Uncertain wording. “What has been entrusted to me” is literally “my deposit” (tēn parathēkēn mou), the banking word of 1 Timothy 6:20. It can mean what Paul has entrusted to Christ (his life, his soul) or what Christ has entrusted to Paul (the gospel). Verse 14 uses the same word for the gospel entrusted to Timothy, which favours the gospel: Christ will guard his own message. But “whom I have believed” suits Paul’s life committed to Christ and kept safe until the last day. Both are true, and perhaps the breadth is deliberate: everything a man cannot hold on to himself, lodged with someone who can.

verseByVerse.quote: Follow the pattern of the sound words that you have heard from me, in the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. By the Holy Spirit who dwells within us, guard the good deposit entrusted to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must keep to the gospel in the shape he received it from Paul, holding it with faith and love, and guard it as a treasure in trust, by the Holy Spirit who lives in him. He is not left to keep it in his own strength.

The pattern of the sound words. “Pattern” (hypotypōsis) is an outline to work from (1 Timothy 1:16): not Paul’s sentences to repeat word for word, but a fixed shape to keep, with no new doctrine invented. “Sound” is the medical word: health-giving. And “that you have heard from me” is the chain this letter keeps tracing: entrusted to Paul, heard by Timothy, handed on to faithful men (2:2), and now preserved for us in Scripture.

Faith and love. Not holding correct doctrine coldly, but with faith and love (Ephesians 4:15). Doctrine kept without them becomes exactly what the Ephesian teachers had: correct-sounding material producing envy and friction.

Guard the good deposit. A deposit is something valuable left in another person’s care. Here it is the gospel (as in 1 Timothy 6:20), to be handed back exactly as it was received. Not developed, not improved. Returned.

By the Holy Spirit. This clause makes the command bearable. Timothy is timid, Paul is about to die, and Asia has deserted; but the guarding is done by the Holy Spirit, who dwells in the man set on guard, as faith dwelt in Lois (v. 5; Romans 8:9, 11).

The architecture of the chapter. Set the two deposits side by side and the shape appears. In verse 12 Paul has entrusted something to God, and God is able to keep it. In verse 14 God has entrusted something to Timothy, and he must keep it, by God’s own Spirit. The same word is used in both directions, and in both the strength comes from God.

The first keeper of the deposit. Before Timothy was told to guard anything, the Son had guarded a deposit of his own: he gave his disciples the words the Father gave him, and guarded them, so that not one was lost except the son of destruction (John 17:8, 12). The Spirit who helps Timothy guard it is the Spirit Christ sent to bring his words to remembrance (John 14:26).

He lives in the jars himself. The truth that saves us was not invented by us and cannot be kept by us. Councils have erred and churches have fallen, and still the pattern of sound words has come down to us whole, because the Spirit who inspired it guards it. Blessed be the God who entrusts his treasure to clay jars, and then lives in the jars himself (2 Corinthians 4:7).

Isn’t insisting on sound doctrine divisive? Not when it is done in faith and love. The pattern exists to give health; it is false teaching that sickens and divides (1 Timothy 6:3–5). Christians may differ charitably on secondary matters, and this commentary tries to show where. But the gospel itself, who Christ is and how a sinner is saved, is not ours to adjust, any more than a bank clerk may adjust a deposit left in his care. You do not love a sick man by giving him the wrong medicine kindly.

I am not a pastor. How do I guard the deposit? By knowing the gospel well enough to tell it plainly and recognise when it is bent, holding to it when it is unpopular, and handing it on to your children and to a younger believer.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Faithfulness is shown by who stands by Christ’s people when it costs something. Paul sets two examples before Timothy. Almost everyone in Asia turned away from the chained apostle, Phygelus and Hermogenes among them (v. 15). One man, Onesiphorus, was not ashamed of his chains, searched Rome until he found him, and kept refreshing him, as he had served at Ephesus (vv. 16–18). Paul prays that the Lord will show him mercy on that day.
verseByVerse.theology:
Shame, and the Man Who Refused It

‘Ashamed’ runs through the chapter (vv.8, 12, 16). The turning away of verse 15 was most likely personal desertion of a dangerous prisoner rather than apostasy (see the note on v. 15).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Asia, the scene of Paul's most fruitful work, turned away at the end (see the note on v. 15).

Now: Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found a condemned man (v.17), an answer to shame available to anybody.

verseByVerse.quote: You are aware that all who are in Asia turned away from me, among whom are Phygelus and Hermogenes.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul tells Timothy plainly that almost everyone in Asia has deserted him, and names two of them. Before he asks Timothy to come, he puts the cost on the table.

All who are in Asia. Asia was the Roman province whose chief city was Ephesus, where Paul spent three years, until all the residents of the province had heard the word (Acts 19:10). It was perhaps his most fruitful work. And at the end, they turned away from him (apestraphēsan, deserted, disowned).

Phygelus and Hermogenes. Two names, appearing once in Scripture, and it is here, for this. Perhaps they had been prominent leaders whom Timothy would otherwise have trusted. Their only memorial is that they turned away.

What all means. “All” may mean a large number, or those from Asia who had been in Rome and failed to stand by Paul at his trial (4:16); either way, it is how things looked from the cell. It reads as personal desertion rather than abandonment of the faith: people who had genuinely believed decided they could not afford to be connected with a prisoner on a capital charge. That is a more ordinary failure, and a more likely one.

Why tell Timothy this? Because Paul is about to ask him not to be ashamed (v. 8) and to come (4:9, 21), and he tells him first that everybody else has declined. He does not make the invitation look more attractive than it is: count the cost first, as Jesus said (Luke 14:28).

The road his Master walked. Paul is not the first to be left by those he had poured his life into. On the night Jesus was arrested, the men he had taught for some three years all left him and fled (Mark 14:50). And at Paul’s own hearing no one came to stand by him, but the Lord stood by him and strengthened him (4:16–17). The Christ who was deserted is the Christ who does not desert. He knows what it is to be left alone, and he was with Paul in that cell.

In everyday life. Who is suffering for Christ and feeling abandoned: the missionary whose newsletter you no longer read, the church member who took an unpopular stand? Do not be the one who turns away. Call, visit, or write.

Christians have let me down badly. How should I respond? Grieve honestly, as Paul does, and name what happened truthfully, without inflating it. Then commit them to God, as he does, and pray that it may not be counted against them (4:16). Forgiveness does not mean pretending trust is unchanged; you may need to be careful with people who have proved unreliable. But do not let their failure define the church for you, or Christ. Paul’s gaze moves straight from the deserters to Onesiphorus, and from both to the Lord who stood by him. And each of us has, at some point, been a Phygelus to someone.

Should we name people who have failed? Rarely, and only for a reason. Paul names Phygelus and Hermogenes not for sport but to inform Timothy, who needed to know whom he could rely on. That is the test: is naming someone true, and necessary to protect others or the gospel? Gossip names people to enjoy their fall; love names them only when silence would leave someone else exposed.
verseByVerse.note: Asia was the Roman province in western Turkey whose chief city was Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, for he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains, but when he arrived in Rome he searched for me earnestly and found me— may the Lord grant him to find mercy from the Lord on that day!—and you well know all the service he rendered at Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Against the deserters stands one man, Onesiphorus, who was not ashamed of Paul’s chains but searched Rome until he found him, and Paul prays that the Lord will show him and his household mercy. He is the living answer to the chapter’s charge.

The household of Onesiphorus. We know Onesiphorus only from these verses and a greeting in 4:19, and he is unforgettable. His name means help-bringer, and he lived up to it. Some think he had died, since Paul prays for his household and greets them without him.

He often refreshed me. Refreshing has to do with cooling (anepsyxen), like the relief of shade or water in a stifling place. And not once but often: a man in a Roman cell was regularly revived because Onesiphorus kept turning up.

Not ashamed of my chains. The chapter’s word for the third time, and here it is answered. Everyone in Asia had been ashamed; this man was not, and he is the model for Timothy (v. 8). Paul specifies the chains: the visible, humiliating, incriminating fact that others could not stomach.

He searched for me earnestly. This detail makes the portrait. Rome held perhaps a million people; a prisoner awaiting trial was listed nowhere convenient, and asking after a man on a capital charge drew official attention. Onesiphorus made exactly the enquiries a sensible man would avoid, until he found him.

Mercy on that day. Onesiphorus searched and found Paul; now Paul prays that he may find mercy. The repeated word is probably deliberate. “That day” is the day of judgment (v. 12).

The service at Ephesus. The man who refreshed Paul in Rome had been quietly serving for years, and Timothy had seen it. Faithfulness in a crisis is usually grown in ordinary days.

A visit the Judge will remember. On that day Christ sits as judge (4:1, 8), and he has already said what he will remember: “I was in prison and you came to me,” and what they did for the least of his brothers they did for him (Matthew 25:36–40). Onesiphorus went looking for a chained apostle; without knowing it, he was visiting Christ. He did not earn mercy by it, for the people Jesus commends there were already “blessed by my Father” (Matthew 25:34). But not one of his searches through the streets of Rome went unseen.

Found by mercy. Onesiphorus searched a hostile city until he found a man in chains, and in that he looks like his Lord. The Son of God came into a far more hostile world, looking for prisoners, and did not stop until he found them; the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost (Luke 19:10). He was not ashamed of our chains. He took them, and broke them. And on that day mercy will be found by people who were first found by mercy.

How can I be an Onesiphorus? Look for the person others are avoiding, and go: the prisoner, the patient on a long-stay ward, the elderly saint who no longer gets to church, the pastor under attack. Go more than once, because “often” is Paul’s word. Take something practical, a meal, a book, news, an errand done, and do not be embarrassed to be seen there. If the person is hard to reach, keep asking until you find them. You need no gift for preaching, only a pair of feet and the willingness to be associated with someone in chains.

How do I thank God for a believer who has died? Gladly, and often: for what he gave you through that person, for the grace that was visible in them, and that they are now with Christ, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). You may speak of them to God with love and tell him your grief; he is the God of all comfort. What Scripture does not give us is any instruction to pray for their condition to be improved (see the box below). Your prayers are better spent on the family they left behind, as Paul’s first prayer here was for the household.

Where Christians differ: does this verse support prayer for the dead? Roman Catholic teaching uses this verse, if Onesiphorus had died, together with 2 Maccabees 12, to support prayers for the dead and the doctrine of purgatory. This commentary’s view: It is not certain that Onesiphorus had died; he may simply have been away from home. Even if he had, Paul’s words are a grateful wish, not a prayer to change a soul’s condition. At death believers go at once into the presence of Christ (Philippians 1:23; 2 Corinthians 5:8; Luke 23:43), and our eternal state is settled at death (Luke 16:26; Hebrews 9:27). There is no purgatory, for Christ’s sacrifice has fully paid for the sins of believers (Hebrews 10:14). So we do not pray for the dead to be released from punishment, though we may thank God for them. Christians who pray for their dead usually do so out of love, and the love is right; Scripture’s comfort is better still, for a believer who has died needs nothing more.
