keyVerse.quote: But I am not ashamed, for I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me.
keyVerse.note: The chapter asks Timothy not to be ashamed, and here Paul shows him how it is done: not by strength of character but by knowing a person. His confidence rests on whom he has believed, not on how firmly he believes, and on what Christ is able to guard, not on what Paul can hold. Every other charge in the chapter flows from this trust.

1.reflection:
Paul says Timothy’s faith came to him through his grandmother and mother (v. 5). Who passed the faith on to you, and to whom are you passing it on? What would it look like to be a Lois or a Eunice to someone?

Paul answers fear not with “be braver” but with the gospel of verses 9–10: saved by grace given before time began, and death abolished. Why is doctrine a better cure for fear than willpower? Which phrase in those verses helps you most?

Being “ashamed” of the gospel or of suffering Christians (vv. 8, 12, 16) rarely means open denial. What does it actually look like in your work, family or friendships, and what does “I know whom I have believed” (v. 12) change about it?

Onesiphorus searched Rome until he found a man in chains (vv. 16–17). Who in your church or community is easy to avoid, and how could you, or we together, be an Onesiphorus to them this month?

2.title: Soldier, Athlete, Farmer: The Shape of Gospel Ministry
2.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 1 called Timothy not to be ashamed but to guard the good deposit, when “all who are in Asia” had turned away from Paul (1:15). Chapter 2 shows what that means day by day: how Timothy is to keep going himself, and how he is to deal with the men in Ephesus who are spoiling the faith of others.

The message. The gospel must outlive its messengers, so hold on to Christ and hand it on, whatever it costs. Strength for the task is grace received, not courage manufactured. The hardship is worth bearing because Jesus Christ is risen and his word cannot be chained. And error is defeated not by winning quarrels but by a man who handles the word straight, keeps himself clean and corrects opponents gently, leaving their repentance to God.

Why it was said. Timothy was young, inclined to timidity, and facing teachers who said the resurrection had already happened (v. 18), while Paul, chained as a criminal, would soon be dead (see the introduction). What happens to the gospel, and to a frightened man, when the apostle is gone?

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–7: be strengthened by grace, entrust the teaching to faithful men, and accept hardship like a soldier, an athlete and a farmer. Verses 8–13 give the reason: Jesus Christ is risen, his word cannot be chained, God’s chosen will be saved through it, and Christ stays faithful to the faithless. Verses 14–19 set word-fights and chatter that spreads like gangrene against the worker who cuts the word of truth straight, on God’s foundation that stands. Verses 20–26 turn to Timothy himself: cleanse yourself to be useful, flee youthful passions, and correct opponents gently, hoping God will grant them repentance.

Where it leads. The chapter’s centre is a person: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David” (v. 8). He refused the crown without the cross; he is the grain of wheat that died and became a harvest, the Lord who knows those who are his, the stronger man who frees the devil’s captives. Beneath it all lies the deepest comfort of the letter: when we are faithless, “he remains faithful”, because “he cannot deny himself” (v. 13).

For us. Every believer has received a gospel someone else suffered to hand on. Go to Christ for strength before the task, not after the failure; expect it to cost something; pass on what you have received; and meet error with the open Bible and a gentle voice, for only God can change a heart.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — A Good Soldier of Christ Jesus
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Timothy is to take his strength from grace, hand the gospel on and accept hardship for it, because Jesus Christ is risen and stays faithful. Verses 1–2 name the source of strength, grace in Christ, and the task, a chain of faithful teachers. Verses 3–7 give three pictures of costly service: the soldier’s single loyalty, the athlete’s lawful race, the farmer’s long labour. Verses 8–10 give the reason: a risen Lord, a word no chains can hold, and chosen people who will be saved through it. Verses 11–13 seal it with a trustworthy saying whose last line rests everything on Christ’s faithfulness rather than ours.
verseByVerse.theology:
The Broken Symmetry of Verse 13

The hymn's first three lines match our action with his response; the fourth breaks the pattern in our favour: ‘he cannot deny himself’ (see the note on vv. 11–13).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Paul arranges for the deposit to pass through four generations of faithful men (see the note on vv. 1–2).

Now: Soldier, athlete, farmer (vv.3–6): single-mindedness, discipline and patience; and the word of God is not bound (v.9).

verseByVerse.quote: You then, my child, be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus, and what you have heard from me in the presence of many witnesses entrust to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must draw his strength from Christ’s grace and pass the gospel on to faithful men who will teach others, so that it outlives Paul.

Be strengthened. “You then” (sy oun) sets Timothy against those who deserted Paul (1:15). The verb (endynamou) means not “be strong” but “be strengthened”, and keep on being strengthened. Paul does not tell a timid man to find strength in himself; he tells him to receive it, and names where it comes from.

By the grace. Grace does not only pardon; it gives strength: “My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9). And it is found in Christ Jesus, from whose fullness we have all received, grace upon grace (John 1:16). Grace is not a store Timothy carries about but a Person he is joined to.

Many witnesses. The apostolic teaching was delivered publicly, unlike the false teachers’ claims to a special knowledge (1 Timothy 6:20). Its truth could be checked, and it still can.

Entrust to faithful men. Entrust is the deposit word again (parathou; 1:12, 14), and the one qualification is faithful (pistois): not gifted, clever or impressive, but reliable. In context the “men” are probably those who will teach in the church, the elders.

Able to teach others. Count the links. Paul heard it from Christ; Timothy heard it from Paul; Timothy is to entrust it to faithful men; they will teach others. Four generations in one sentence: from a death cell Paul is arranging for the gospel to outlive him. A man who receives the truth but does not pass it on is a dead end, however sound he is.

The chain has never broken. The risen Christ entrusted his gospel to fishermen and a converted persecutor, and he has never once let the chain break. That is how the faith reached you: through a long line of people, most of them unrecorded, who received it and handed it on.

What does being strengthened by grace look like in practice? Going to Christ for strength before the task, not after failing at it: taking in his word and prayer at the start of the day like food, not as a duty to tick; remembering what grace has already done (forgiven, adopted, sealed); confessing sin quickly, so that nothing blocks the supply; and using the means he gives, the preaching of the word, the Lord’s Supper and the fellowship of believers. Grace seldom feels like a surge of power. It feels like being able to do the next right thing, and then the next.

I am not a teacher. Does verse 2 involve me? Yes. Any believer can be faithful: pray for those who teach, support their training, and test what you hear. And the chain runs through ordinary relationships: parents teach children, older women train younger women (Titus 2:3–5), friends explain the gospel to friends. The teaching office in the church belongs to qualified men, the elders; this commentary holds that complementarian view because Paul ties the office to qualified men (1 Timothy 2:12; 3:1–2), while many faithful Christians read those passages differently and welcome women as pastors. Both agree that the duty of passing on what you have received belongs to every believer, man or woman. Someone handed it to you. Whom could you hand it to?

Where Christians differ: is this apostolic succession? Roman Catholic, Orthodox and some Anglican traditions teach that the bishops form an unbroken line from the apostles, through which authority and grace are passed by ordination. This commentary’s view: What is passed on here is the apostolic teaching, not an office or a sacramental power. True succession is succession in doctrine: those who faithfully teach what the apostles taught stand in the apostolic line, and a man ordained in an unbroken line who teaches error is no successor of the apostles (Galatians 1:8–9). The apostolic deposit is now held in Scripture. Many in those traditions love the apostolic gospel; the disagreement is over where its authority now lives.

verseByVerse.quote: Share in suffering as a good soldier of Christ Jesus. No soldier gets entangled in civilian pursuits, since his aim is to please the one who enlisted him.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s worker must accept hardship like a soldier on active service, kept free of whatever would stop him pleasing the one who enlisted him.

Share in suffering. The same compound verb as 1:8: suffer together with. Three pictures follow in quick succession: the soldier, the athlete and the farmer.

A good soldier. Roman soldiers endured hard training, long marches, poor food and danger, and the Christian worker must expect the same (Philippians 2:25). But Paul chooses the soldier for one quality, named in the next verse.

Entangled in civilian pursuits. “Entangled” (empleketai) means caught as in a net, and “civilian pursuits” are literally the affairs of life: not sinful things but ordinary ones, business, property, domestic arrangements. Roman soldiers on active service were expected to keep clear of trade. They accepted a limit on how much ordinary life they could carry, because they could be moved at any hour.

The one who enlisted him. Christ enlisted us; we did not appoint ourselves. He did it not because we were promising recruits but because he had already won the war, and he did it at a price (1 Corinthians 6:19–20). Our aim is to please him (2 Corinthians 5:9). A soldier has exactly one person to satisfy, which simplifies a great many decisions; for Timothy, in a church full of people with opinions about him, that is a considerable relief.

What it does not mean. It does not mean ministers may never work at a trade; Paul himself made tents (Acts 18:3). Nor does it make ordinary work unspiritual for other Christians, or excuse neglecting your family: Paul has just insisted that a man manage his own household well and provide for his relatives (1 Timothy 3:4; 5:8). The warning is against being so woven into comfort and property that you cannot be moved when the order comes.

How do I know whether something is an entanglement? Ask three questions. Does it compete with Christ for my first loyalty, so that I find myself pleasing it, or the people attached to it, rather than him? Does it make me unavailable for what he clearly asks? Would I put it down tomorrow if he required it? Good things become entanglements by growth, not by nature: the second job, the house project, the hobby, the online world. Your family is not an entanglement but a calling (1 Timothy 5:8); yet even good duties must be carried so as to leave you a soldier, not a civilian.

verseByVerse.quote: An athlete is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules. It is the hard-working farmer who ought to have the first share of the crops. Think over what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in everything.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Christ’s work must be done his way and for the long haul, like an athlete who keeps the rules and a farmer who waits for the harvest.

According to the rules. “Crowned” (stephanoutai) refers to the victor’s wreath, and the condition is exact: “according to the rules” (nomimōs, lawfully). At Olympia athletes swore they had trained for ten months and would keep the rules, and a man could win the race and be disqualified for what he had done beforehand. There is a right way to do Christ’s work, with holiness, truth and endurance, and effort spent any other way wins no crown.

The hard-working farmer. Hard-working is the labouring word, work to exhaustion (kopiōnta), and the farmer adds what the other two lack: time. A soldier’s battle is decided in a day, an athlete’s race in an afternoon; a farmer works for months and sees nothing. Ministry is like that, but there will be fruit, and the worker will share in it (1 Corinthians 9:7–11).

Think over what I say. Paul does not explain the three pictures. He tells Timothy to work at them (noei, reflect on), and then promises that the understanding will be given. Hard thinking is commanded; understanding is God’s gift (Proverbs 2:1–6). The man who waits for insight without labouring will not get it, and the man who labours as though it depended on his own cleverness has misunderstood where it comes from.

The crown without the cross refused. The athlete’s temptation, to take the crown by another route, was once offered to Christ himself. The devil showed him all the kingdoms of the world and offered them for a single act of worship (Matthew 4:8–10): the crown without the cross. Jesus refused, and ran the course his Father set, through Gethsemane and Golgotha; he is now crowned with glory and honour because he suffered death (Hebrews 2:9). Every shortcut in ministry is a small echo of that offer, and Timothy’s crown will be given by the Lord who ran first and kept every rule (4:8).

The God of the long harvest. He waited long ages for the fullness of time, and then sent his Son as a seed into the ground: unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone, but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). That one seed has become a harvest no one can number. Blessed be the Lord of the harvest, never in a hurry and never late.

What it does not mean. The athlete’s crown does not mean we earn salvation by keeping rules; the crown is the reward God graciously gives to faithful service (4:8; 1 Corinthians 9:25). Nor does the farmer’s share mean ministry is about financial gain.

What if I have worked for years and seen no fruit? Then you are a farmer in the long months, and this verse is for you. Fruit in God’s work is often invisible, delayed or harvested by someone else: one sows and another reaps (John 4:37–38). Faithfulness is your responsibility; growth is God’s (1 Corinthians 3:6–7). Check honestly that the seed is the word of God and the method is not compromise; then keep sowing, and leave the calendar to him. Many a missionary has died before the church he planted grew, and many a mother never saw her prayer for her son answered in her lifetime. Your labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58).

How do I think over Scripture? Read a passage slowly, more than once. Ask what it says, what it meant to the first readers, and what it shows about God and about Christ; notice the images and the connecting words. Pray for the understanding he promises. Carry a verse through the day and turn it over, the way a cow chews the cud. Use good helps, a sound commentary, your pastor’s preaching, but do not let them do all your thinking.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel, for which I am suffering, bound with chains as a criminal. But the word of God is not bound!
verseByVerse.commentary:
In every hardship Timothy must keep Jesus Christ in view, risen from the dead and David’s promised son, for this gospel cannot be chained even when its preacher is.

Remember Jesus Christ. “Remember” (mnēmoneue) is present tense: keep him in view. Under pressure the things you know perfectly well slip from the mind, and the remedy is to call them back deliberately, which is what the Lord’s Supper is for. In hardship the greatest encouragement is not a technique but a person.

Risen from the dead. Raised and still risen (egēgermenon): not an event that happened and was over, but the state he is in now. There is a risen man, and nothing will ever make him unrisen.

The offspring of David. Two clauses, and they are the whole gospel in shorthand. Risen: so he is Lord and death is beaten. Offspring of David: so he is truly human, the promised King, and the promises to Israel have been kept in him (2 Samuel 7:12–16; Romans 1:3–4). Paul calls it “my gospel” not because he invented it but because it was entrusted to him (1 Timothy 1:11).

In the flow. The soldier, the athlete and the farmer all accept hardship now for something that comes later, and in Jesus Christ that pattern is seen in full: suffering first, then resurrection. And when Hymenaeus and Philetus deny a future resurrection (v. 18), this verse has already answered them.

As a criminal. “Criminal” (kakourgos) is the word Luke uses of the two men crucified beside Jesus (Luke 23:32–33). Paul is classed with the worst, and so was his Lord.

The word of God is not bound. A strong “But” (alla) sets the chained man against the word that cannot be chained (dedetai, bound). Rome can hold the apostle and can do nothing whatever to the message; it goes on spreading (Philippians 1:12–14; Isaiah 55:11). The sentence written in that cell has travelled further than any of the men who put him there. The chains are dust, and Nero is a name in a history book. Preachers can be silenced, buildings closed, Bibles confiscated; the word itself has never been imprisoned by anybody.

How do I remember Jesus Christ in practice? Bring him to mind deliberately, especially when pressure makes you forget. Read the Gospels regularly, so that your picture of him is filled from Scripture, not your moods. Come to the Lord’s Supper as a remembrance, not a ritual. Sing about him. When anxious, tell yourself the two facts of this verse: he is risen, so death and evil do not have the last word; he is David’s son, so every promise of God has come true in him (2 Corinthians 1:20). Remembering is not nostalgia but letting the facts of the gospel rearrange the facts of today. When your situation feels like a cell, a diagnosis, a job you cannot leave, the word of God is not bound there either; and pray for believers imprisoned for their faith today, by name if you can.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus with eternal glory.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul bears everything gladly because God has chosen people who will be saved, and the gospel he suffers for is how they will be reached.

I endure everything. Because the word is not bound, Paul’s suffering is worth it. “Endure” (hypomenō) is staying put under a load rather than escaping it, and “everything” is no rhetoric from this man: floggings, stonings, shipwrecks (2 Corinthians 11:23–28), and now chains, cold (4:13), betrayal and approaching death.

For the sake of the elect. Not for his own reward, but for people, most of whom he has never met and some not yet born: those whom God chose before time began (1:9), including those not yet converted, whom God will call through the gospel. Paul does not know who they are, but he knows they exist, and so he knows his suffering will not be in vain.

That they also may obtain. If God has chosen a people, why endure anything? In Scripture election is never a reason for inaction; it is the reason action is worth taking. God ordains both the end, salvation, and the means: preaching, suffering, prayer. Because Paul knows God has chosen people, his labour is not a gamble; because he does not know who they are, he preaches to everyone (Acts 18:9–10).

With eternal glory. Everything endured is weighed against what it leads to: this light momentary affliction is preparing an eternal weight of glory beyond all comparison (2 Corinthians 4:17).

Other sheep I have. Paul’s confidence about people he has never met is borrowed from his Lord, who said he had other sheep not yet in the fold, who would listen to his voice (John 10:16). The Shepherd laid down his life for them before most of them were born, and he gathers them now by the voice of his gospel in the mouths of men like Paul. Not one name the Father wrote in the Lamb’s book of life will be missing on the last day, and so Paul’s suffering is never wasted.

Does election mean someone might want to be saved and be turned away? No. Scripture never pictures a person longing for Christ and being refused because he was not chosen. The invitation is genuine and universal: “whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37); “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (Romans 10:13). By nature no one seeks God (Romans 3:11), so where a real desire for Christ appears, it is itself the sign that God is drawing that person. Election is not a wall keeping seekers out but the reason there are any seekers at all. So preach freely to everyone, and if you are wanting Christ, come.

Why should I put up with hardship for people I do not know? Because Christ did, and because they are his. Paul loved the Lord who had chosen them, and knew the gospel would reach them only if someone carried it. That is the logic of every missionary, every faithful Sunday school teacher, every believer who gives to send the word where he will never go. The hardship may be small: an awkward conversation, money you would rather keep, time with a difficult person. It is never wasted, because at the other end of it is someone God has chosen and is calling.

verseByVerse.quote: The saying is trustworthy, for: If we have died with him, we will also live with him; if we endure, we will also reign with him; if we deny him, he also will deny us; if we are faithless, he remains faithful— for he cannot deny himself.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A trustworthy saying sets out what is at stake: those united to Christ will live and reign with him, those who finally deny him will be denied, yet our failures cannot undo his faithfulness.

The saying is trustworthy. The fourth of the five trustworthy sayings, with the rhythm of a hymn, perhaps a confession said at baptism: four lines each beginning with “if”, and they do not all run the same way.

If we have died with him. “Died with” (synapethanomen) is a past tense pointing to one event: our union with him in his death, which takes place when we come to faith and is signified in baptism (Romans 6:3–8); it may also include martyrdom, and Paul writes on the eve of his own. Christ died as the representative of everyone joined to him by faith, so God counts his death as theirs, and the old life under sin’s rule and the law’s condemnation is over, as a debt is over once paid (Romans 6:6–7; Galatians 2:20).

If we endure. The tense is present: keep enduring. And the promise is startlingly large: not mere survival but reigning (symbasileusomen; Romans 8:17). No believer endures perfectly; Christ endured perfectly in our place, and his obedience is counted as ours (Romans 5:19), so our faltering endurance is accepted for his sake, not weighed as if we were earning our place.

If we deny him. Then the line turns dark, with the Lord’s own word: whoever denies me before men, I also will deny before my Father who is in heaven (Matthew 10:33). This is a settled, final rejection of Christ, and it has a settled, final answer.

He remains faithful. In the fourth line the pattern breaks, and it breaks in our favour. We might expect: if we are faithless, he will be faithless to us. Instead, we are faithless, and he remains faithful. The ground is not our sincerity but Christ’s nature: to abandon his people or break his promises would be to deny himself, and that is the one thing he cannot do (Numbers 23:19; Titus 1:2). Written to a frightened man by a dying one, there is hardly a more reassuring sentence in the letter.

Denying and failing. To deny is to disown deliberately and finally; to be faithless is to fail, to be the sort of Christian who keeps collapsing. Peter’s denials on the night of Jesus’ arrest were the faithlessness of a frightened man, not a settled rejection of Christ, and the difference between him and Judas was not the size of the failure but what happened afterwards. Jesus had prayed for Peter that his faith would not fail (Luke 22:31–32), and it did not.

He would have to stop being himself. Here is the steadiness of the Son of God. We are brave on Sunday and silent on Monday, and through every failure he stays exactly what he has always been. Our grip on him slackens a hundred times, and his grip on us never once. Blessed be the faithful Christ, who would have to stop being himself before he could let us go.

In everyday life. When you have failed him again this week, and you will, say the fourth line to yourself, and then get up and go on. When you are tempted to soften your loyalty to him to avoid trouble, say the third line, and let the warning keep you.

I once denied Christ, or hid my faith, when I was afraid. Am I lost? If you are troubled by it now, that is very strong evidence that you are not. The denial this verse warns about is a settled, final repudiation, the kind that does not grieve and does not return. Peter swore he did not know Jesus, and within weeks he was preaching at Pentecost. Do what Peter did: weep over it, confess it plainly, and come back. Jesus met Peter on the shore with a fire and breakfast and asked him three times, do you love me (John 21:15–17), one question for each denial. He has not changed: if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us (1 John 1:9).

What does it mean that we will reign with him? Sharing in Christ’s rule as his people. In part this is already true: believers are seated with Christ in the heavenly places (Ephesians 2:6), and the souls of the martyrs reign with him now while they wait for the resurrection (Revelation 20:4). That last reading is the amillennial one this commentary holds: the thousand years of Revelation 20 picture the present age between Christ’s two comings, because the book speaks throughout in symbols. Many faithful Christians (premillennialists) expect a literal thousand-year reign on earth after his return; all agree that his people will reign with him. Its fullness comes at his return, when they inherit the new creation (Matthew 25:34; Revelation 22:5). It is not a reward for being impressive but the destiny of those united to the King.

Where Christians differ: if Christ remains faithful, can a believer still be denied? Some take the third and fourth lines as contradictory: either believers can be lost (line three), or not (line four). Arminian Christians (who hold that saving grace can be resisted and finally lost) read the third line as a warning that real believers may fall away, out of reverence for the warning. Others take the fourth line as a threat: he remains faithful to his warnings and will judge the faithless. This commentary’s view: Line three describes final, deliberate apostasy, which reveals that a person never truly belonged to Christ (1 John 2:19); such people will be disowned. Line four describes the weakness of genuine believers, who sometimes falter, doubt or fail, like Peter. Christ’s faithfulness to them does not depend on their strength; he keeps them, and so they do not finally deny him (John 10:28–29; Luke 22:31–32). The warning is real, and is one of the means by which Christ keeps his people from apostasy; the comfort is real, and is the ground of their perseverance.
verseByVerse.note: The fourth of the “trustworthy sayings,” perhaps an early hymn.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–26 — A Worker Approved by God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Error is not met by winning quarrels but by a worker who handles God’s word straight, keeps himself clean and corrects opponents gently. Verses 14–18 set word-fights and spreading chatter, seen in Hymenaeus and Philetus, against the approved worker who cuts the word of truth straight. Verse 19 sets God’s unshakeable foundation against the damage. Verses 20–22 turn to Timothy himself: in a house of mixed vessels, cleanse yourself and pursue godliness in good company. Verses 23–26 describe the Lord’s servant, kind, patient and gentle, because only God can grant repentance and free the devil’s captives.
verseByVerse.theology:
Cutting Straight

‘Rightly handling’ (v.15) is to cut straight: accuracy, not eloquence (see the note on v. 15). And God's foundation bears a seal with two inscriptions (see the note on v. 19).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Hymenaeus, already disciplined (1 Tim 1:20), was still teaching that the resurrection had come, wrecking the hope of the grieving first (see the note on vv. 16–18).

Now: Word-fights damage the hearers (v.14); cleanse yourself rather than audit the house (v.21); and correct with gentleness, since repentance is God's to grant (v.25).

verseByVerse.quote: Remind them of these things, and charge them before God not to quarrel about words, which does no good, but only ruins the hearers.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must keep reminding the church of these truths and solemnly forbid quarrels about words, which help no one and wreck the faith of those who listen.

Remind them. Keep reminding (hypomimnēske) the faithful men and the church of the truths of verses 1–13. Much of ministry is reminding people of what they already know (2 Peter 1:12–13).

Charge them before God not to quarrel about words. “Charge” (diamartyromenos) is solemnly warn, as in 1 Timothy 5:21. Paul does not treat word-fighting (logomachein), the disease diagnosed in 1 Timothy 6:4, as a minor irritation to be managed; he charges the church about it in the sight of God.

Ruins the hearers. It is useful for nothing (ep’ ouden chrēsimon), and it ruins the hearers: katastrophē, the collapse of a structure, our word catastrophe. See who suffers: not the combatants, who are usually enjoying themselves, but the people in the room who did not want the fight. Somebody there is new in the faith, or barely holding on, and learns that Christianity is a thing people shout about. The participants go home invigorated; the hearers go home with their faith damaged.

The hearers Christ guards. Paul has his Lord’s warning behind him: whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in him to stumble would be better off drowned in the depths of the sea (Matthew 18:6). When the Sadducees brought Jesus a trick question about a woman married seven times, he did not play their word game; he took them back to the Scriptures and the power of God, the living God of Abraham (Matthew 22:23–33), and the crowd went away astonished at his teaching, not worn out by a quarrel. That is the alternative to word-fighting: an answer that leaves the listeners seeing God more clearly.

How do I tell a word-fight from a necessary argument for the truth? Look at the subject, the spirit and the fruit. Is this about the gospel and what Scripture clearly teaches, or about a speculation, a label, or a point Scripture leaves open? Am I trying to help someone see the truth, or to win, to be seen winning, or to vent? Would I be as eager if no one were watching? Is anyone being built up, or are people being unsettled and divided? Paul argued hard for justification by faith (Galatians 2:11–14) and for the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15), and contending for the faith is right (Jude 3). Fighting about words for the pleasure of fighting is not. Before you join an argument, online or at church, picture the quiet listener who never says anything, and speak as though that person were the one you were answering.

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to present yourself to God as one approved, a worker who has no need to be ashamed, rightly handling the word of truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must work hard to win God’s approval as a workman whose work stands inspection, by teaching God’s word accurately.

One approved. “Do your best” (spoudason) means make every effort. This is not God’s acceptance of Timothy as righteous, which he already has in Christ, but a master’s approval of a workman’s work, and the one whose approval counts is God, not the congregation or the critics. “Approved” (dokimos) is the word for metal tested and passed as pure. And the shame word of chapter 1 is turned round: Timothy must not be ashamed of the gospel, and his own labour must give him nothing to be ashamed of, like a craftsman whose work holds up under inspection.

Rightly handling the word of truth. Rightly handling is cutting straight (orthotomeō), the word used in the Greek Old Testament of a straight path (Proverbs 3:6). Paul, a tentmaker (Acts 18:3), may have known the picture from his own trade: the material is expensive, and a crooked cut cannot be uncut. The idea is accuracy, so that people are led straight. “The word of truth” is the gospel and the whole of Scripture.

Accuracy, not eloquence. Between the word-fights of verse 14 and the empty chatter of verse 16, Paul sets not a cleverer argument but the plain word, accurately taught: what is actually there, not what the preacher would like to be there. The word-fighters use Scripture as ammunition; the approved worker handles it like a man who will answer for every cut.

Where the straight cut leads. The word of truth is, in Paul’s phrase, the gospel of your salvation (Ephesians 1:13), and that tells the workman where every straight cut ends. Jesus said of the Scriptures, it is they that bear witness about me (John 5:39). A crooked handling of the Bible never arrives at him, or arrives only by forcing the text. Paul asks not for clever links but for the real line of Scripture, from promise to fulfilment, followed honestly. Cut the text straight and it leads to a cross and an empty tomb, because that is where God laid the road.

What it does not mean. It does not mean only scholars can understand Scripture; its main message is clear to all (Psalm 19:7). Nor is “rightly dividing” (KJV) a call to divide Scripture into separate dispensations, as the phrase has sometimes been used. The verb means cutting straight, handling correctly, as the ESV’s “rightly handling” shows.

I do not teach the Bible publicly. How do I handle the word rightly? Everyone who reads the Bible, teaches a child or shares a verse with a friend is handling it. Do it straight. Read whole passages, not isolated lines. Ask who wrote it, to whom and why, before asking what it means for you. Let clear passages explain unclear ones. Notice how the passage points to Christ, for the whole Bible is about him (Luke 24:27). Be careful about lifting a promise made to someone else and claiming it unchanged. When you do not understand something, say so rather than force a meaning onto it. A plain, careful reading is far better than a clever, crooked one.

verseByVerse.quote: But avoid irreverent babble, for it will lead people into more and more ungodliness, and their talk will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have swerved from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already happened. They are upsetting the faith of some.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must stand clear of godless chatter, because it spreads like gangrene, as the claim of Hymenaeus and Philetus that the resurrection has already happened is proving. It is overturning the faith of some.

Avoid irreverent babble. Not refute it: avoid it, stand clear of it (periistaso), as in 1 Timothy 6:20. Some error is not worth the dignity of an argument. And there is irony in “lead people into more and more” (prokopsousin, make progress): the false teachers claimed spiritual progress, and they were making it, into ungodliness. Error does not stay mild; each step makes the next one thinkable.

Like gangrene. Paul, who has spoken of healthy teaching throughout these letters, chooses a deliberately unpleasant word: dead tissue that spreads and destroys healthy flesh. It does not stay where it started, cannot be reasoned with, and is treated by cutting away.

Hymenaeus and Philetus. Hymenaeus appeared in the first letter, handed over to Satan that he might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20). If this is the same man, he is still at it and has acquired a colleague: discipline had not, so far, worked, and the New Testament says so without pretending otherwise. “Swerved” (ēstochēsan) is missed the mark, as in 1 Timothy 1:6.

Already happened. Most likely they taught that the resurrection is only spiritual, the new life a believer has now, with no raising of the body still to come. This probably grew from the idea that the body is unimportant (1 Timothy 4:3). It sounds advanced, and it leaves nothing to wait for. Without a bodily resurrection, Christianity is destroyed (1 Corinthians 15:12–19).

Upsetting the faith. “Upsetting” (anatrepousin) is overturning, as one overturns a table. If the resurrection has already happened, the Christians whose bodies are in the ground have missed it, and everyone still suffering has nothing coming (compare 2 Thessalonians 2:2).

A resurrection with nail marks. The teachers were right that one resurrection has already happened, but it was not ours. It was Christ’s, and it was bodily: “a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have,” he told his frightened disciples, and showed them his hands and his feet (Luke 24:39). He rose as the firstfruits (1 Corinthians 15:20), the first sheaf of the same harvest, so a risen body in the past guarantees risen bodies in the future. Make ours merely spiritual, and you have quietly done the same to his. Because he rose, the graves of the saints are not monuments but seed beds.

What it does not mean. It does not deny that believers have already been raised with Christ spiritually (Ephesians 2:6; Colossians 3:1). That is true. The error is saying that is all there is, and denying the future bodily resurrection.

Is full preterism the same error? Full preterism, taught by some today, holds that Christ’s return and the resurrection were fulfilled in AD 70. It differs from partial preterism, held by many orthodox Christians, which sees some prophecies (such as Jesus’ words about the temple) fulfilled in AD 70 while still awaiting his bodily return. Paul’s verdict on Hymenaeus applies to the full form: to say the resurrection has already happened is to swerve from the truth and upset faith. The resurrection of the body is still to come.

How do I avoid error without becoming closed-minded? Being open to learning and being open to anything are different. Stay teachable: test what you hear by Scripture, and be willing to be corrected by it. But you need not give every new idea a hearing, any more than a doctor must try every remedy advertised online. Avoiding godless chatter means not feeding on it: not spending your evenings on teachers who sneer at the Bible or sell novelties. Know the truth well and the counterfeit becomes easier to spot, as bank clerks learn to detect forgeries chiefly by handling the real thing. And if you know someone grieving whose hope has been shaken, remind them gently that the resurrection is still to come, and that it is a resurrection of the body.

verseByVerse.quote: But God's firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: "The Lord knows those who are his," and, "Let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever false teachers overturn, God’s own work stands firm, sealed with two truths: the Lord knows those who are his, and those who are his turn from sin.

God’s firm foundation. Against men who are overturning the faith of some, Paul sets something that cannot be overturned. The foundation is probably God’s church built on his truth (1 Timothy 3:15), or God’s saving work itself, and “stands” (hestēken) is perfect tense: has stood and goes on standing. It does not rest on the reliability of its members, and the weakest believer stands on it as firmly as the apostle. Its seal, a mark of ownership and authenticity, carries two inscriptions facing in opposite directions.

The Lord knows those who are his. The first inscription is God’s side. It echoes Moses’ words during the rebellion of Korah, when God showed who truly belonged to him (Numbers 16:5), and that is Timothy’s situation: respected teachers have defected and nobody is sure who is sound. “Knows” means the love by which God chose them and keeps them as his own (John 10:14; Romans 8:29). You may be badly wrong about somebody. He is not in any doubt.

Depart from iniquity. The second inscription is our side, perhaps echoing the same story (Numbers 16:26). To name the name of the Lord is to profess faith in Christ. You cannot verify who belongs to God, but you can attend to your own conduct: whoever claims the name is thereby committed to leaving the sin.

The name on the seal. For Paul, the Lord of both inscriptions is the Lord Jesus: to name the name of the Lord is to call on Jesus as Lord (Romans 10:9, 13), and the one who knows his own is the Good Shepherd. Some later manuscripts, followed by the KJV, read the name of Christ here; the earliest read the Lord, and for Paul the meaning is the same. The foundation itself rests on him (1 Corinthians 3:11). Heretics can shake people standing in the building; they cannot touch the stone.

Two lines on one seal. Hold the two together and you have the balance the whole New Testament keeps. Assurance rests on God’s knowledge, not on our performance, yet turning from sin is exactly the evidence that a person belongs to him. A foundation with only one of the two lines will not hold a building up.

Someone I trusted as a Christian has fallen away. Was I deceived, and could it happen to me? He may never truly have been the Lord’s, though he looked it (1 John 2:19); or he may be a believer in a terrible fall, whom God will yet bring back. You cannot always tell, and you are not asked to. The Lord knows. As for you, the seal that comforts also directs. Look for assurance not in your skill at spotting frauds, nor in past experience alone, but in Christ, and in the fruit his Spirit is producing now: love for him, hatred of your sin and a continuing turning from it. Those whom the Lord knows, he keeps (John 10:27–29). Then name one iniquity you are tolerating, and depart from it today, practically: remove the access, make the call, or confess to a friend.
verseByVerse.note: The first saying echoes the rebellion of Korah; the second gathers the sense of Moses’ warning to leave the rebels’ tents.

parallels.desc: the LORD will show who is his

verseByVerse.quote: Now in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver but also of wood and clay, some for honorable use, some for dishonorable. Therefore, if anyone cleanses himself from what is dishonorable, he will be a vessel for honorable use, set apart as holy, useful to the master of the house, ready for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The visible church, like a great house, holds both honourable and dishonourable vessels, and Timothy’s part is to keep himself clean, so that he is ready for the Master’s use.

A great house. A large household had gold and silver for the table, and wood and clay for the kitchen, the yard and the jobs nobody describes at dinner. Applied to the church, the household of God (1 Timothy 3:15), the picture explains what Timothy is looking at: the visible church contains a mix of people, and Hymenaeus and Philetus are in the house as dishonourable vessels. Their presence does not mean the house is false.

Cleanses himself. “What is dishonorable” is literally “these” (apo toutōn): the false teachers, their teaching, and the sin that goes with it. Paul does not tell Timothy to sort the house; he tells him to cleanse himself. Faced with a congregation containing frauds, the temptation is to spend your energy inspecting everybody else, and Paul redirects it entirely. And the promise is remarkable: the classification is not fixed. A vessel can change class, and it does so by being cleansed, not by being more gifted or prominent.

Useful to the master. “Set apart as holy” (hēgiasmenon) is a perfect tense: consecrated and remaining so. “Useful” (euchrēston) names a plain ambition, not to be admired or prominent but useful, and “ready” for whatever he requires (3:17). This is sanctification: God setting a person apart as his own, and then making him in practice what he has declared him to be (1 Thessalonians 5:23).

The master who chose a persecutor. Paul knew this from his own life. On the Damascus road he was the most dishonourable article in the house, a persecutor of the church, and the Lord Jesus said of him to Ananias, he is a chosen instrument of mine, literally a vessel (skeuos), to carry my name (Acts 9:15). The master of this house is Christ, and the cleansing that makes a vessel fit for him begins with his washing, not ours (Titus 3:5). The vessel’s own cleansing is real, but it is the response of something already claimed by the master and wanted at his table.

Should I leave a church that has false teachers in it? It depends on where the error is and what the church does about it. Every church has weak and sinful members, and you should not leave because the house contains clay pots; neither did Timothy. Your first duty is to cleanse yourself, and to pray and speak up through proper channels. But if the leaders themselves teach a different gospel, deny essential truths such as the resurrection, or refuse to deal with open error, it is right to seek a faithful church (Galatians 1:8–9). Leave graciously, without gossip, and if possible explain your reasons to the elders.

How do I cleanse myself in practice? By turning from what defiles and coming to Christ who washes. Name the specific things: a habit, a source of false teaching, a relationship that is pulling you into sin. Confess them, receiving his forgiveness (1 John 1:9). Cut off the supply, as Jesus said of the eye that causes you to sin (Matthew 5:29–30), and replace it with what is good (Philippians 4:8). This is not saving yourself but the Spirit at work in you; you do it because you have been washed, not in order to be. And expect the work to be humble: the jobs Christ gives his clean vessels are often small and unseen, a meal cooked, a child listened to, a verse passed on.

verseByVerse.quote: So flee youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace, along with those who call on the Lord from a pure heart.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must run from the passions of youth, including the urge to win arguments, and run after righteousness, faith, love and peace in the company of sincere believers.

Flee youthful passions. “Flee” is run from, as in 1 Timothy 6:11. “Youthful passions” include sexual desire (1 Timothy 5:2), but the next verse is about quarrels, and a young man’s passions also include the appetite for argument, the need to be proved right, impatience, pride and the ambition to make a mark quickly. A young minister facing Hymenaeus and Philetus will want to take them on and win, and Paul lists that instinct among the things to run from.

Pursue righteousness. Four things to chase: righteousness, faith, love and peace, and peace is the pointed one, the opposite of the quarrels in verses 14 and 23.

From a pure heart. The pursuit is not solo. Timothy is to run with those who call on the Lord (epikaloumenōn ton kyrion) from a pure heart (Romans 10:13; 1 Timothy 1:5). Paul’s answer to a young man surrounded by corrosive people is not isolation but better company. You cannot always choose your congregation, but you can largely choose whom you spend time with inside it, and over ten years that choice shapes a person more than almost anything else.

The four are found in Christ. These are not abstract virtues but what Timothy already has in Christ, worked out in his life. Christ Jesus became to us righteousness from God (1 Corinthians 1:30); he is the one in whom faith rests; his love surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19); and he himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Timothy is not running after something he may never reach, but growing into the likeness of the one who has already made him his own (Philippians 3:12).

I am not young any more. Does this verse still apply? Yes. Youthful passions do not check your birth certificate. Many older believers still crave the last word, flare up when contradicted, chase novelty or struggle with lust, and age has its own temptations: bitterness, hardened opinions, love of comfort. The command is the same at every age: run from the sin characteristic of your season of life, and chase righteousness, faith, love and peace with others who love the Lord. Name the passion you most need to flee this week, and decide in advance, praying for the Spirit’s help, what you will do instead when it rises. An older believer who has learned to flee and pursue is exactly the companion a younger one needs.

What if I cannot find such companions? Pray for them, and look harder. They are often quieter than the loudest people in a church: the faithful at the prayer meeting, the older couple who have walked with God for decades, the young believer hungry for Scripture. Invite one person to read the Bible and pray with you, and be the companion you are looking for. If your church truly has none, that may be a sign to seek a healthier one. And you are never entirely alone; the Lord himself walks with those who call on him.

verseByVerse.quote: Have nothing to do with foolish, ignorant controversies; you know that they breed quarrels. And the Lord's servant must not be quarrelsome but kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil, correcting his opponents with gentleness. God may perhaps grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth, and they may come to their senses and escape from the snare of the devil, after being captured by him to do his will.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The Lord’s servant refuses pointless controversies and corrects his opponents with kindness, patience and gentleness, because only God can grant them repentance and free them from the devil’s trap.

Foolish, ignorant controversies. “Have nothing to do with” (paraitou) is refuse. “Foolish” (mōras) gives us moron; “ignorant” (apaideutous) is undisciplined; the controversies are speculative questions, and they “breed” quarrels (gennōsin, a birth word), as Timothy has watched them do.

The Lord’s servant. A title (doulon kyriou) used of Moses, David and the prophets. He must not be quarrelsome, the requirement for an overseer (1 Timothy 3:3). Behind most quarrelsomeness lies a need to be right in order to feel safe, as if our standing depended on winning. The Lord’s servant has been given a righteousness not his own (Philippians 3:9), and a man whose standing is settled in Christ can afford to lose an argument, and even to be thought a fool.

Kind to everyone, able to teach, patiently enduring evil. “Kind” (ēpion) is used of a nursing mother (1 Thessalonians 2:7), and “everyone” includes the opponents. “Able to teach” stands between kindness and patience: the answer to error is not fighting but teaching. “Patiently enduring evil” (anexikakon) is bearing wrong without retaliating, and assumes he will be ill-treated. “Correcting” (paideuonta) is instructing so as to change someone, so gentleness is not vagueness; but it is done with gentleness (prautēs), not harshly, sarcastically or arrogantly.

Grant them repentance. This changes the whole tone of the task. Repentance is God’s gift (Acts 5:31; 11:18), which is why gentleness is not weakness. If the outcome depended on the teacher’s argument, overwhelming force would be the sensible tactic. It does not. No one can argue anybody into the kingdom, so the servant’s job is to correct clearly, treat people well and leave the granting to God. “Perhaps”: we do not know to whom God will grant repentance, but we hope and pray; and the repentance he gives leads on to knowing the truth (1 Timothy 2:4).

The snare of the devil. “Come to their senses” (ananēpsōsin) is become sober again: false teaching clouds the mind like drink. “Captured” (ezōgrēmenoi) is taken alive, as prisoners of war. Paul’s picture of his opponents is not that they are villains but that they are caught, doing somebody else’s will while believing it is their own (most take “his will” as the devil’s). That is why he tells Timothy to be gentle with them.

The stronger man. Gentleness towards captives would be naive if the captor were undefeated. He is not. Jesus said no one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man (Mark 3:27), and at the cross he disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame (Colossians 2:15). Everyone who comes to their senses and walks out of the devil’s trap is plunder taken back by a stronger hand. So the Lord’s servant can afford to be patient: he is not breaking the snare by the force of his own argument, but speaking the word through which the risen Christ still frees his prisoners.

Captives set free, drunkards made sober. This is how God dealt with us. We were opponents, captives of the devil, drunk on our own wisdom, and he did not overwhelm us with force. He sent his Son, gentle and lowly in heart, who prayed for those who crucified him. Then he granted us repentance and woke us up. Every believer is a captive set free and a drunkard made sober. Glory to the God whose kindness leads the hardest heart home.

What it does not mean. It does not mean never being firm or never confronting error; Paul is firm throughout. Confrontation is to be done with gentleness, patience and hope. Nor does “God may perhaps grant them repentance” mean human response is not real; people do repent, but they repent because God grants it.

How do I correct someone with gentleness? Begin with yourself: pray before you speak, and ask honestly whether you want to win or to help. Go to the person rather than talking about them, in private if you can. Ask questions first, so that you understand what they actually believe. Then say what is true plainly, give your reasons from Scripture, and stop; you do not need the last word. Keep praying, for verse 25 puts the outcome in God’s hands. The gospel makes this possible. Timothy Keller often pointed out that it makes a person humble and confident at once: humble, because you are saved by grace and not by being right, so you cannot look down on anyone; confident, because you are loved in Christ, so you do not need the other person’s agreement to feel secure. And remember where you came from (see “Captives set free, drunkards made sober” above).

Are people in error to blame if the devil has captured them? Yes. Captivity here is not an excuse; they are opponents of the truth and must repent, which means turning from something they are responsible for. But it is a reason for compassion. We too once followed the prince of the power of the air (Ephesians 2:1–3), and were freed not by our cleverness but by grace. The person who opposes you is not your real enemy but a prisoner of your real enemy (Ephesians 6:12). Hate the trap, pity the captive, and pray by name to the God who sets prisoners free, that he will grant this one repentance.

Does gentleness mean I must keep arguing with someone forever? No. Gentleness governs how you correct, not how long. Paul says to have nothing to do with foolish controversies (v. 23), and elsewhere to warn a divisive person once and then twice, and after that have nothing more to do with him (Titus 3:10). You may decline a debate that has become a quarrel, end a conversation kindly, or stop feeding someone who only wants to fight. What you may not do is become harsh, sarcastic or contemptuous. Say what is true, say it kindly, pray, and leave the outcome with God.

keyVerse.quote: Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David, as preached in my gospel
keyVerse.note: This verse stands at the centre of the chapter and of the whole letter. The soldier, the athlete and the farmer all accept hardship now for what comes later, and in the risen Son of David that pattern is complete; the denial of the resurrection in verse 18 is answered before it is raised. When pressure drives everything else from a believer’s mind, this is the one thing to keep in view.

2.reflection:
Verse 1 tells Timothy not “be strong” but “be strengthened by the grace that is in Christ Jesus.” What difference does it make to go to Christ for strength before a hard task rather than after failing at it? What would that look like in your week?

Verse 2 describes four generations passing on the gospel. Who handed it to you, and to whom could you hand it on, at home, in the church or among friends?

The soldier, the athlete and the farmer (vv. 3–6) each show a different side of costly faithfulness. Which picture speaks most to where you are now? What entanglement or shortcut is most likely to pull you off course?

Verses 24–26 call for kindness, patience and gentleness towards opponents because only God can grant repentance. How should that change the way we disagree with others, in the church, at home and online?

3.title: Perilous Times and the God-Breathed Word
3.overview:
Where we are. Chapter 2 ended with Timothy correcting opponents gently, in the hope that God would grant them repentance. Chapter 3 steps back to show the age in which that work is done, and then tells Timothy what will hold him steady in it, before the final charge to “preach the word” in chapter 4.

The message. The last days, which began with Christ, will bring fierce times, and the worst danger will wear the clothes of religion. Do not be surprised and do not be moved: stay with the truth you were taught, for Scripture is God’s own breath, able to make you wise for salvation in Christ and to equip you for every good work. The answer to savage times is not novelty but the word God has already spoken.

Why it was said. Paul was about to die, many in Asia had turned away, and in Ephesus teachers with a convincing outline of godliness were working their way into homes (see the introduction). A young and timid man might well wonder whether the gospel was losing, and whether he needed something newer or more impressive to meet the moment.

How the chapter makes its case. Verses 1–9 paint the times: nineteen marks framed by love of self and love of pleasure, describing not pagans but religious people with the appearance of godliness and none of its power, who prey on the burdened and, like Pharaoh’s magicians, imitate the truth until God exposes them. Verses 10–13 set Paul’s life against theirs: teaching and conduct watched at close range, persecutions at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra, and the Lord who rescued him from them all, with the flat promise that all who desire to live godly lives will be persecuted while impostors go from bad to worse. Verses 14–17 give Timothy his anchors: the people from whom he learned, and the sacred writings he has known from childhood, which are breathed out by God and profitable for every part of the Christian life.

Where it leads. Paul’s list of vices is the exact negative of Jesus Christ, who did not please himself but emptied himself. The power of godliness the imitators lack is the living Christ at work by his Spirit. The Lord who rescued Paul from every danger had himself refused rescue at the cross, so that he could save others. And the Scriptures make a person wise for salvation only “through faith in Christ Jesus” (v. 15): every page of the God-breathed book is leading somewhere, and the destination is him.

For us. We live in the same last days. Expect them to be hard, and expect the subtlest danger to be religion without reality, in others and in ourselves. Find faithful believers whose lives you can watch, and keep the open Bible at the centre of your life and your church, read with faith in Christ. It is what God has given, and it is enough.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Godlessness in the Last Days
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the last days people will love themselves instead of God, and the most dangerous of them will look godly. Paul lists the marks of love turned inward, from lovers of self to lovers of pleasure (vv. 1–4); shows that it can wear the outline of religion while denying its power (v. 5); exposes how such teachers creep into homes and take the burdened captive, keeping them always learning but never arriving (vv. 6–7); and promises that, like Pharaoh’s magicians, they can imitate the truth only for a while before God sets a limit and their folly is plain to all (vv. 8–9).
verseByVerse.theology:
What ‘the Last Days’ Means

The last days began with Christ, and Timothy was living in them (see the note on v. 1). The list's final item puts the whole catalogue inside the church (see the note on v. 5).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The vices are framed by self-love and pleasure-love, and mostly describe relationships breaking down (see the note on vv. 2–4).

Now: Imitation has a ceiling: Pharaoh's magicians could not keep pace for long (see the note on vv. 8–9).

verseByVerse.quote: But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Expect fierce seasons in the age between Christ’s comings, and know that each one is fixed on God’s calendar.

But understand this. Paul’s pastoral method is to warn in advance (1 Thessalonians 3:4). A Christian told to expect savage times is not destroyed by them; one promised an easy road is.

That in the last days. They began with Christ’s coming and the outpouring of the Spirit (Acts 2:16–17; Hebrews 1:2), because God’s final word has been spoken in his Son: after Christ comes nothing new, only Christ again, returning. Timothy was living in them, or he could hardly “avoid such people” (v. 5).

There will come times of difficulty. “Difficulty” (chalepoi) means fierce; its only other New Testament use is of the two demoniacs so fierce that no one could pass that way (Matthew 8:28): times with teeth in them. And the word for “times” means appointed seasons: the hard stretches come and go through the age, each one on God’s calendar, not ours.

The Lamb holding the scroll. The Lord of history is never taken by surprise; he told his church before the first persecution what the age would be like. Above all the savagery of men sits the Lamb who was slain, holding the scroll of history and opening its seals one by one (Revelation 5). The seasons of difficulty are his, and they are numbered.

So should I expect the world simply to get darker until Christ comes? Expect both darkness and light, for the wheat and the weeds grow together until the harvest (Matthew 13:30). Christians should not be naive about seasons of fierce godlessness; but this is also the age of the gospel running to the nations, while Christ builds his church. So the right posture is neither panic nor optimism about culture, but steadiness: we were told, we know who holds the calendar, and the King is coming. Pessimism about the world is never permission for idleness in the gospel.

Where Christians differ: are the last days only at the end of history? Some, especially dispensationalists (who see God’s plan unfolding in distinct eras, with a separate future for Israel), place the last days only in a short period just before Christ’s return. This commentary’s view: Scripture treats the whole church age as the last days, beginning at Pentecost, for Peter and Hebrews both say they have already begun. Throughout this age there will be seasons of great difficulty and godlessness, which may intensify before Christ’s return (2 Thessalonians 2:3). This is the amillennial view: the present age is a time of gospel advance and of opposition until Christ comes once, visibly, to judge and to renew all things. (Amillennial means reading the thousand years of Revelation 20 as Christ’s present reign rather than a future earthly kingdom.) Many faithful Christians, premillennial and dispensational, read the end-time passages differently, and this commentary honours them as brothers; Paul’s point to Timothy stands whichever way they are read.
verseByVerse.note: The “last days” began with Christ’s first coming.

verseByVerse.quote: For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy, heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good, treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,
verseByVerse.commentary:
When love turns inward, away from God, every relationship begins to come apart. Paul’s list is love aimed at the wrong things, at self, money and pleasure instead of God and neighbour.

For people will be lovers of self. Eighteen items in three verses (nineteen with v. 5), framed by lovers of self and lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God; everything between is what those two produce. Paul begins not with atheism but with the self turned inward, the great commandment reversed (Matthew 22:37–39).

Lovers of money. It follows at once, as so often in these letters (1 Timothy 6:10). Then the outward pride: proud, arrogant, and “abusive”, literally blasphemers, whose speech tears others down.

Disobedient to their parents. Then relationships break down, the heart of the list: the fifth commandment rejected, thanklessness, unholiness. “Heartless” is the loss of the affection that binds a family without anyone having to try. “Unappeasable” is a treaty word: the person who refuses the truce and will not accept an apology.

Slanderous. This is the very word for the devil (diaboloi), the accuser of the brothers. Then the loss of restraint: without self-control, brutal, not loving good. “Treacherous” is the word used of Judas (Luke 6:16), and “swollen with conceit” describes a man puffed up and blinded by pride (1 Timothy 3:6).

Lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God. The list ends as it began, with misdirected love. Not that pleasure is evil, for God “richly provides us with everything to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17), but that it has taken God’s place.

What the list is not. There is scarcely anything here about false doctrine, and nothing about persecution: just ordinary relationships coming apart, in families, gratitude, affection, promises and self-restraint. The difficult times will look less dramatic than we imagine and more recognisable, and some of these traits can appear in believers too.

Everything this list is not. The Son of God did not love himself at the expense of others; he emptied himself. He gave thanks on the night he was betrayed, prayed for his executioners and laid down his life for his friends. He was everything this list is not, and he gives himself to people who were everything it is. That is also the cure, for love turned inward cannot be mended by another list. Christ “died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him” (2 Corinthians 5:15). Self-love is not argued out of a person but displaced, when a greater love takes hold (1 John 4:19), and the cross is the one sight that can turn a heart’s love outward again.

Amused rather than oppressed. We usually picture the threat to faith as hostility. Paul ends somewhere quieter. In Amusing Ourselves to Death Neil Postman set two warnings side by side: Orwell feared we would be ruined by what we hate, a state that bans books; Huxley, by what we love, a culture so entertained that nobody wants to read one. Postman thought Huxley the better prophet, and he wrote before the phone in your pocket. A life can be filled to the edges with small pleasures, none of them wicked, and leave no room for God, simply because it never got round to him. The answer is not to give up pleasure, which God made, but to meet a love that outweighs it. On the cross Jesus refused the wine mixed with myrrh that would have dulled the pain (Mark 15:23). We reach for whatever will numb us; he stayed awake to bear the whole weight of our sin, so that we need not live distracted from God, or die without him.

In everyday life. Ingratitude is the quietest item on the list and perhaps the commonest: a meal eaten without thanks, a kindness taken as owed. The cure can begin small: a word of thanks to God for something specific, and to the person who did it, said aloud.

Does “lovers of self” condemn healthy self-regard? No. Paul condemns the self-absorption that puts self at the centre, not the ordinary self-care Jesus assumes in the command to love our neighbour as ourselves (Matthew 22:39). The call to build self-esteem can feed the very self-love Paul describes; the gospel gives something better, a secure identity in Christ that frees us to forget ourselves.

I see some of these traits in myself. Am I one of these people? Reading the list as a mirror rather than a weapon is a good sign. Every believer has remnants of these sins: ingratitude, love of comfort, an unforgiving streak. The people Paul describes are characterised by them, their lives organised around self, and they are content to be. A Christian has begun to love God more than self, and fights what remains. So neither dismiss the list nor despair over it: take the trait you recognise to Christ, who loved God perfectly in your place and is remaking you in his image.

What if my parents ask me to sin, or are abusive? Disobedience to parents here means the contemptuous rebellion that throws off all honour, not refusing to do wrong. We must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), parents included, and no one may take part in sin because a parent demands it. Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden; it should be reported, and the vulnerable protected. Honour can then take the form of prayer, respectful speech and care in need as far as is safe, even when obedience is not possible and distance is necessary.

verseByVerse.quote: having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid such people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The deadliest form of this godlessness is religious: it keeps the outward shape of godliness while refusing the power that changes a life.

Having the appearance of godliness. This nineteenth item makes the list terrifying. Verses 2–4 could describe the pagan world outside the door; this clause puts the whole list inside the church. “Appearance” (morphōsis) is an outline, the outward shape of a thing. These people attend worship, use Christian language, perhaps even teach, and would be offended to be told they were not Christians.

But denying its power. What is missing is power (dynamis), the work of the Spirit that actually changes people. They may recite the creed accurately and deny its power by lives that stay unchanged (Titus 1:16). The form attracts because it can be kept without surrender: the comfort and respectability of religion with self still on the throne. That is as possible in a sound church as in a false one.

Avoid such people. Present tense: keep turning away; do not argue them down or give them a platform (2:16). Paul means not struggling Christians or people whose lives are a mess, but settled hypocrisy, kept up deliberately, and Timothy is not to pour his effort into it. Nor are forms of worship bad; the problem is form without power.

Godliness has a name. The mystery of godliness is Christ, “manifested in the flesh” (1 Timothy 3:16), and its power is not religious energy but the living Christ at work by his Spirit. Take him from the centre and the outline of religion stands for a while, but it can no longer change anybody. God is not content with the outline of a Christian. He wants, and he creates, the real thing: new hearts, changed lives, a people who love him.

In everyday life. The power of godliness is the Spirit who raised Jesus, living in every believer. Ask him to make it real in one area this week, your speech at home perhaps. It will be real but never perfect, and need not be: Christ obeyed perfectly in your place, and for his sake God gladly accepts your halting obedience.

How do I know whether my own faith is only an appearance? Ask what it is doing, not only what it says. Is Christ changing how you treat your family, use money, speak about people, act when no one is watching? Do you pray without an audience? Do you grieve over your sin, or only over being caught? Power here is not spectacular experience but the Spirit’s quiet work of making you like Christ. If you find mostly form, do not try harder at the form: go to Christ, confess the emptiness, and ask for the life only he gives; he does not turn away those who come. That you are asking at all is a sign of the Spirit at work, for the people Paul describes are untroubled by the question.

Does “avoid such people” mean cutting off family members who are like this? Not in the sense of abandoning ordinary duties. Paul means chiefly religious influence in the church: do not follow them, give them a platform or let them shape you. You still owe family members love, honesty and, where it is safe, kindness, and you may pray for their conversion. But a hypocritical relative need not set the spiritual direction of your home, teach your children or draw you into his ways, and where there is manipulation or abuse, appropriate distance is right.

verseByVerse.quote: For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Such teachers prey on the burdened, slipping into homes and keeping their followers always learning but never arriving at the truth.

Those who creep into households. The verb means to slip in unnoticed. The churches met in households, and a man with religious credentials could get into a home as he never could into a public gathering, and work there without oversight.

And capture weak women. “Capture” is a war word, the picture of 2:26. “Weak women” is literally “little women”, with a note of contempt, though not for women as such: Paul credits Lois and Eunice with Timothy’s faith (1:5) and counts women among his fellow workers (Romans 16:1–7). He means particular women who had become easy targets, vulnerable rather than stupid.

Burdened with sins. This is the profile predators have always looked for: someone heaped up with guilt and pulled by desires in several directions. A person weighed down by what they cannot resolve will listen to anybody who offers relief, true or false.

Always learning. Every new class, every new idea, but never full knowledge (epignōsis; compare 1 Timothy 1:4). A certain kind of teaching is designed to produce learning that never arrives, because a person who arrives no longer needs the teacher.

The truth they never reached. The knowledge of the truth has a destination, and it is a person: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6; Ephesians 4:20–21). To arrive would have meant laying the heaped-up load of sin on the one who “bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). Learning that never reaches Jesus is not a slow road to the truth but a road around it.

Liberty to the captives. False teachers creep into houses to take captives; Christ came openly “to proclaim liberty to the captives” (Luke 4:18). He did not trade on anyone’s guilt; he carried it. A woman bent double for eighteen years he called a daughter of Abraham and set free (Luke 13:11–16): a Shepherd who lifts the heaviest load off the weakest back.

What it does not mean. Not that women are more easily deceived than men in general: Paul is describing particular women in Ephesus, and the false teachers who preyed on them were men. Nor does it make continued learning bad (2 Peter 3:18).

How do I protect myself and others from teachers like this? Watch for the marks Paul gives: entry by stealth rather than through the church’s oversight; a focus on the guilty and lonely; teaching that keeps you dependent rather than settled; novelty that never brings repentance and faith in Christ. Today they creep in through screens as well as doors: the online teacher with secret insight, the course that never ends, the counsellor who isolates you from your church. Stay joined to a local church and its elders. Bring your guilt to Christ, who lifts it freely, so that no one can trade on it. And if someone vulnerable is being drawn in, go to them gently, and tell your elders.

I keep learning but never feel settled. What should I do? Ask whether your learning is aimed at obeying. Settled knowledge comes from submitting to what God has plainly said, and the plain things are enough to begin with: who Christ is, what he has done, what he commands. Narrow your diet for a season: one good church, one book of the Bible read slowly, one sound book on the gospel. Act on what you know. And settle the main thing: have you come to Christ in repentance and faith? Endless learning is sometimes a way of avoiding the one step that would end the search.

verseByVerse.quote: Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith. But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Like Pharaoh’s magicians, these men can imitate the truth for a while, but God sets a limit, and in the end everyone sees their folly.

Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses. The names are not in the Old Testament; Jewish tradition gave them to Pharaoh’s magicians (Exodus 7:11, 22), and Paul uses a tradition his readers knew without endorsing all it contained. The comparison is exact: the magicians did not deny Moses; they reproduced what he did. Their opposition was imitation, the very danger of men with the outline of godliness (v. 5).

So these men also oppose the truth. “Disqualified” (adokimoi) is the metal-testing word in the negative: tested and rejected (Titus 1:16). Timothy is to present himself approved (2:15); these men have failed the test.

But they will not get very far. Here is the mercy in the passage: a limit. In 2:16 such men advance in ungodliness; here there is a point they cannot pass. Not that the trouble will be brief: Hymenaeus, disciplined in the first letter (1 Timothy 1:20), was still at work (2:17).

For their folly will be plain to all. Egypt’s magicians matched Moses through two plagues, then could not produce gnats, and had to tell Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8:18–19). Imitation runs out, usually sooner than the watchers fear. Every counterfeit in history comes at last to its gnats, the point where it has nothing more to show, and the finger of God is seen.

The finger of God. When Jesus was accused of casting out demons by Satan’s power, he answered that if he did it by the finger of God, the kingdom of God had come upon them (Luke 11:20). He is the greater Moses (Hebrews 3:3): the magicians could imitate a plague, but no one could imitate the man who came back from the dead. Counterfeits can copy the outline of his works for a time, but not him, and sooner or later the difference shows.
