In everyday life. Ask of any impressive ministry not whether it can do what the real thing does, but whether it leads people to Christ crucified and to holy lives.

Why does God let false teachers succeed for a time? Scripture gives several reasons. Error reveals who is genuine (1 Corinthians 11:19). It drives the church to understand the truth more clearly; many of the great creeds were written in answer to it. It teaches believers to depend on God’s word rather than on impressive people. And it gives time for repentance, even to the false teachers themselves (2:25). None of this makes error good, but God is sovereign over it and sets its limit: they will not get very far.
verseByVerse.note: Jannes and Jambres are not named in Exodus; Jewish tradition gave these names to Pharaoh’s magicians.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–17 — Scripture and the Man of God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Against the imitators, Timothy is to stay with the real thing he has been given: the life he has watched and the Scriptures God has breathed out. He has seen Paul’s teaching and conduct proved through stones and scars, and the Lord’s rescue in them all (vv. 10–11); persecution is the normal lot of the godly, while deceivers go from bad to worse (vv. 12–13). So he must continue in what he learned from those he trusts and from the sacred writings, which make him wise for salvation through faith in Christ (vv. 14–15) and, being God-breathed, equip him completely for every good work (vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Breathed Out by God

Scripture is God-breathed (v. 16): it proceeds from him, though not by dictation, and it makes the man of God complete (see the note on vv. 16–17).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Lystra, where Paul was stoned (v. 11), was Timothy's home (see the note on vv. 10–11).

Now: Opposition for godliness (v. 12) is not evidence of failure (see the note on vv. 12–13).

verseByVerse.quote: You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness, my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra—which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy has watched the real thing in Paul: a life that matched its teaching through suffering, and a Lord who rescued him every time.

You, however, have followed. The “you” is emphatic, and the chapter turns on it. Against the imitators stands one young man who has had the real thing in front of him for years. “Followed” is the word for a disciple keeping pace with a teacher (1 Timothy 4:6).

My teaching, my conduct. One item of doctrine, then eight of character and experience: his aim in life, his faith, his patience with people, his steadfastness in hardship. Timothy came to know Paul not chiefly from lectures but on the road, watching how he behaved and how he took it when things went wrong.

At Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra. The towns of the first missionary journey, Lystra being Timothy’s home (Acts 16:1). This is Pisidian Antioch, where Paul and Barnabas were driven out of the district (Acts 13:14, 50), not the Syrian Antioch that sent them out. At Lystra Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city for dead (Acts 14:19); Timothy may well have watched him get up and walk back in. He knew from the start that following Christ meant suffering.

From them all the Lord rescued me. Sometimes by escape, sometimes by healing, always by his presence (2 Corinthians 1:10). Paul writes from a cell, knowing he will not be rescued this time, and says it anyway, because the Lord will bring him safely into his heavenly kingdom (4:18): the execution will complete the rescue, not cancel it. The stones of Lystra could not keep Paul down, and the sword of Rome will not keep him dead.

The Rescuer who was not rescued. The Lord who brought Paul out of Antioch, Iconium and Lystra had himself refused rescue. In Gethsemane he could have asked his Father for more than twelve legions of angels (Matthew 26:53), and he did not. At the cross the mockers said, “He saved others; he cannot save himself” (Matthew 27:42). He would not save himself, because he was saving others. Every rescue Paul lists was bought by that refusal, and so is the last one, through the sword and into the heavenly kingdom.

In everyday life. Most of us have a Lystra somewhere behind us, a trouble the Lord brought us through: an illness, a debt that was met, a dark year that ended. Remembering them is not nostalgia but evidence, the same evidence Paul offers Timothy.

Whom should I follow? Look for what Timothy saw in Paul: sound teaching joined to a life that matches it, watched over time and in hardship. Not the most famous voice online, but believers near enough to watch at home, with money, in suffering and in speech. Your elders should be such people (1 Timothy 3:1–7; Hebrews 13:7). Follow them as they follow Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), never uncritically and never in his place. And remember that someone may be watching you.

God did not rescue someone I love from illness or death. Did he fail them? No, any more than he failed Paul when the sword fell. His rescue comes sometimes as escape, sometimes as strength to endure, and for every believer finally as deliverance through death into his presence, which is far better (Philippians 1:23). That does not make the loss less painful, and Scripture does not ask you to pretend it is; Jesus wept at a grave. But the believer you lost has been rescued in the fullest sense, brought safely into the heavenly kingdom beyond the reach of any harm. He who did not spare his own Son did not abandon them.
verseByVerse.note: Timothy came from Lystra, where Paul was stoned and left for dead.

verseByVerse.quote: Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted, while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everyone who sets out to live for Christ will meet opposition, while deceivers sink deeper into their own deception. Opposition for godliness is not evidence of failure; it is the normal lot of the godly.

All who desire to live a godly life. Verse 12 widens Paul’s own story into a rule for every believer, flat and unqualified: all. And what draws opposition is not being godly but desiring to be, so nobody can conclude they are not godly enough for the verse to apply.

Will be persecuted. A promise, not a possibility (John 15:18–20; 1 Peter 4:12–14), to be read honestly rather than dramatically: most Christians in comfortable countries will not be imprisoned, and pretending otherwise cheapens the word for those who are. But its ordinary forms are familiar: the family that finds you embarrassing, the promotion your convictions cost you, the friendships that quietly cool.

From bad to worse. Verse 13 tells the opposite story. “Impostors” first meant sorcerers and by Paul’s day swindlers, a glance back at Jannes and Jambres. They make progress too, in the wrong direction; verses 14–17 tell Timothy what to hold on to while they do.

Deceiving and being deceived. The deceiver is himself deceived: tell untruths long enough and you lose the ability to tell (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11), and from the inside you cannot see it. But the anxious may take comfort: a believer who fears being deceived and goes to Scripture to be corrected is not in that state, for the self-deceived do not ask.

Persecuted in Christ. The godliness that draws fire is Christ’s own life showing in his people, and the hostility is aimed at him. Paul learned that on the Damascus road, as the persecutor: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). The Lord who suffered first counts his people’s blows as his own, and having told us we would share his treatment, he tells us to take heart, for he has overcome the world (John 16:33).

What it does not mean. Not that persecution is proof of godliness; some suffer for their own wrongdoing (1 Peter 4:15). Nor that Christians should seek persecution or be needlessly offensive.

I am not persecuted at all. Does that mean I am not living a godly life? Not necessarily, but ask honestly. God gives seasons of peace (Acts 9:31), opposition is light in some places and roles, and it is often quieter than we notice. But if your faith never costs you anything, ask whether anyone around you knows you are a Christian, and whether you ever take a stand that would be unpopular. The aim is not to provoke opposition, but to be so plainly Christ’s that, when it comes, it finds you on his side.

How should I respond when I am opposed for my faith? As Jesus taught: do not retaliate, but bless those who curse you and pray for those who mistreat you (Luke 6:27–28). First be sure it is for righteousness, not rudeness (1 Peter 3:15–17; 4:15). Rejoice, strange as it sounds, for you share in Christ’s sufferings and your reward in heaven is great (Matthew 5:11–12). Let your church carry it with you. Use lawful protections where you have them, as Paul appealed to Caesar. And keep doing good: the best answer to slander is a life that makes it implausible (1 Peter 2:12).

verseByVerse.quote: But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Timothy must stay with the truth he was taught, held by the people who taught it and by the Scriptures, which lead to salvation through faith in Christ.

But as for you, continue. The contrast again, and now the instruction: remain. Against a world going from bad to worse, Timothy is not told to innovate but to stay where he is, in the truth, kept there by the Spirit who dwells within us (1:14). He has not merely heard it; he has “firmly believed” it.

Knowing from whom you learned it. Two reasons follow, the two grounds on which anyone holds the faith. The first is personal. The pronoun is plural in the best manuscripts (some later ones, followed by the KJV, have the singular): Paul, and also Lois and Eunice (1:5). Timothy knows what the teaching made of them. That is an argument from evidence, not authority: when doctrine is under pressure, part of what steadies a person is the memory of believers whose lives could not be explained any other way.

From childhood. The second reason is the text itself. The word means infancy, and the “sacred writings” are the Old Testament. Two women taught a small boy the Scriptures, and years later Paul points to it as the reason Timothy will stand firm when everyone else defects.

Which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. The Scriptures do not merely inform; they lead to salvation, through faith in the Christ to whom the Old Testament points (Luke 24:27; John 5:39). Ignore where it points and you can know the sacred writings very well and not be saved by them, like many of Paul’s opponents (2 Corinthians 3:14–16).

In everyday life. A bedtime Bible story can look like a small thing. Lois and Eunice probably thought so too, and it held a man steady when an empire turned against him.

How do I continue when others are moving on? Continuing sounds passive, but it is a choice made every day. Read the Scriptures themselves, not only books about them. Stay planted where the word is faithfully preached, even when a newer voice seems more exciting. Test doubts and new ideas slowly against Scripture, talking them over with mature believers, before you let them move you (Acts 17:11). Remember those whose lives showed you the truth, and go back often to the plain centre: Christ died for our sins, was raised, and is coming again. Above all, remember who is doing the keeping: “no one will snatch them out of my hand,” Jesus said (John 10:28). Your grip on him matters, but his grip on you is what lasts.

How does the Old Testament make anyone wise for salvation through Christ? By showing us who God is, what sin is and what he promised to do about it, and pointing to the one who would do it. The sacrifices taught that sin must be paid for by a substitute; the Passover lamb, the scapegoat and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 showed what kind. David’s line pointed to the King; the law showed that we cannot save ourselves. So Timothy recognised Jesus when Paul preached him: he had been taught what to look for. Read the Old Testament still as the long promise, and Christ as the yes to every promise.

I was not taught the Scriptures as a child, or my teachers failed me. What then? Begin now: the Scriptures can make you wise at forty as well as at four, for the power is in God’s word, not in the reader’s age. If those who taught you proved hypocrites, that hurts, but Paul’s second reason stands on its own: the Scriptures themselves, read with faith in Christ. Find faithful believers to watch and learn from now. And give your children or grandchildren what you were not given; many a family’s line of faith begins with one person who started late.

verseByVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Every part of Scripture comes from the mouth of God, and so it is useful for every part of the Christian life and enough to equip God’s servant for all he is called to do.

All Scripture. Every part of it: not only what moves you, but the genealogies, the building specifications, the psalms that call down judgment. Paul means first the Old Testament, the sacred writings of verse 15, the part of the Bible Christians most often quietly shelve.

Is breathed out by God. God-breathed (theopneustos): a very rare word, which Paul may have coined. Not God-inbreathed, as though he breathed life into documents that already existed, but God-outbreathed: Scripture proceeds from him as breath from a speaker (Psalm 33:6; Matthew 4:4). The older word “inspired” now suggests a writer in a heightened mood, as we say of a poet. The claim is about origin: what Scripture says, God says.

Not dictation. Luke researched (Luke 1:3), Paul argues and sometimes writes in hot anger (Galatians 5:12), David bleeds all over the Psalms. Peter puts both halves together: men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit (2 Peter 1:20–21). The men really spoke, and the Spirit really carried them, so that what they wrote is exactly what God intended.

Profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness. Because it is from God, it is useful, and four uses follow in two pairs: teaching shows what is right, reproof what is not, correction how to get right, and training (paideia, the word for raising a child) how to stay right. Scripture does not stop at diagnosis; a reader who only ever feels rebuked by the Bible is using half of it.

That the man of God may be complete. “Man of God” was the title of Moses and the prophets, used of Timothy in 1 Timothy 6:11, and by extension of every believer who belongs to God. “Complete” means fully fit for purpose.

Equipped for every good work. Fully fitted out, like a ship supplied for a voyage: no task God gives lies beyond what Scripture equips us for. This is the sufficiency of Scripture, and the answer to the whole chapter. Against savage times, imitators, predators in households and deceivers going from bad to worse, Timothy is handed a book: not a technique, a strategy or secret knowledge.

The Lord who trusted every word. The strongest reason to receive Scripture as God-breathed is that the Son of God did. “Scripture cannot be broken,” he said (John 10:35); he met temptation with it, went to the cross in obedience to it, and said that everything written about him must be fulfilled (Luke 24:44). He promised that the Spirit would guide his apostles into all the truth (John 16:13), and so the New Testament stands beside the Old. To receive the Bible as God’s word is not to rank a book above Christ but to share his own view of it, and to hear in every part the God who speaks of him.

God is not silent. The breath that spoke the stars into being has breathed out a book, and in it God speaks to us as a father to his children. He has not left us to grope for him in the dark or to lean on the shifting opinions of men. Heaven and earth will pass away, but his words will not (Matthew 24:35).

What it does not mean. Inerrancy does not mean reading every passage literally regardless of genre; poetry, parable and prophecy are read as what they are. And sufficiency does not mean Scripture tells us everything about everything, such as science or medicine, but everything we need for salvation and godliness (2 Peter 1:3).

In everyday life. The Bible on the kitchen table is the voice of God, as truly as the voice at Sinai, only gentler. A short prayer before reading, “Lord, correct me today”, turns a habit into a meeting with God.

Does “All Scripture” include the New Testament? Paul means first the Old Testament Scriptures Timothy knew from childhood (v. 15). But the New Testament treats the apostles’ writings as Scripture too: Peter puts Paul’s letters with “the other Scriptures” (2 Peter 3:16), and Paul quotes a saying of Jesus found in Luke 10:7 as Scripture (1 Timothy 5:18). The same breath of God stands behind both Testaments.

What about the apparent contradictions and errors people point to? Take them seriously, and humbly. Many dissolve on careful reading: writers report different details of one event, round numbers, arrange material by theme rather than date, or speak of the sunrise as we still do. Others come from the history of copying, which responsible Bibles note openly; the text is preserved with remarkable care, and no doctrine depends on a doubtful reading. A few remain hard, and it is honest to say so. But God does not lie, and two centuries of scrutiny have seen many confident claims of error answered by archaeology and better understanding. Keep reading, ask for help, and give God the benefit of the doubt you would give a trusted friend.

Is it not circular to trust the Bible because it says it is from God? Every final authority is in that position: whatever could certify it would be the higher authority, and even reason cannot prove itself without using reason. But the claim does not hang in the air. It comes with a risen Lord who treated these writings as his Father’s word (John 10:35), with promises made centuries ahead and kept in him, with one message running through some forty writers and fifteen centuries, and with changed lives. Above all, the Spirit who breathed it out opens blind eyes to its glory, so that a believer trusts it as he trusts the sun, by its own light (1 Corinthians 2:12–14).

How do I read the Bible so that it does all four things in me? Read it regularly, and all of it over time. Come expecting God to speak, and ask four questions of each passage: What does this teach me about God? Where does it show me I am wrong? How does it set me right, especially through Christ? What habit of righteousness does it train me in? Read with others, under good preaching, so that you are not just reading your own opinions back into it. Then obey, for training in righteousness happens in practice, not in the armchair. The Bible is not a book you master; it is a book through which God masters you.

Does the sufficiency of Scripture mean I should not see a doctor? No. Scripture is sufficient for what it was given for: to make us wise for salvation and to equip us for godliness, including the struggles of heart and mind. It no more replaces medicine than it replaces plumbing; Paul told Timothy to take a little wine for his stomach (1 Timothy 5:23), and Luke was a physician. Medical care is a gift of God’s common grace. So if you are struggling, seek out a biblical counsellor through your church, or if it has none, through a biblical counselling organisation (for example ACBC or CCEF in the US, Biblical Counselling UK in Britain), and tell your pastor. A good biblical counsellor will ask you to have a medical check-up, so that any bodily cause is found and treated, and will then help you work through the struggle itself from God’s Word, which is sufficient for what you face. If the doctor recommends treatment, receiving it is not a failure of faith. Sufficiency means that nothing else may overrule Scripture on who you are, what is right and wrong, and how to be reconciled to God. Use every good help, and test every help by the word.

Where Christians differ: is Scripture alone the final authority? Roman Catholic and Orthodox teaching holds that Scripture and tradition together, interpreted by the church, are the rule of faith. Liberal Protestantism (which reads the Bible chiefly as a record of human religious experience) holds that Scripture contains God’s word but also human error. Some charismatics look for ongoing revelation alongside Scripture. This commentary’s view: Because all Scripture is God-breathed, it is entirely true and without error in all it affirms (inerrancy), for God cannot lie (Titus 1:2; John 17:17). Because it equips the believer for every good work, it is sufficient: we need no further revelation or tradition of equal authority to know what to believe and how to live. Scripture alone is the supreme and final authority for faith and practice (sola Scriptura). Tradition, creeds and teachers are valuable servants, but they must be tested by Scripture and corrected by it (Acts 17:11). And the canon is closed: the apostolic deposit is complete (Jude 3; Hebrews 1:1–2). Many charismatic brothers agree that nothing they receive may add to Scripture or overrule it, and this commentary gladly recognises that common ground while holding that the revelatory gifts belonged to the apostolic foundation.

Uncertain wording. The first clause of verse 16 has no verb in Greek, so it can be read “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable” (the ESV and most translations) or “Every God-breathed Scripture is also profitable” (some older translations). Even the second does not imply that some Scripture is not God-breathed, and the natural way to take the “and” (kai), as joining two things said of Scripture, favours the first. Pasa may also mean “every” (each passage) rather than “all” (the whole); either way no part of Scripture falls outside God’s breath.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>But understand this, that in the last days there will come times of difficulty.<sup>2</sup>For people will be lovers of self, lovers of money, proud, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy,<sup>3</sup>heartless, unappeasable, slanderous, without self-control, brutal, not loving good,<sup>4</sup>treacherous, reckless, swollen with conceit, lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God,<sup>5</sup>having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power. Avoid such people.<sup>6</sup>For among them are those who creep into households and capture weak women, burdened with sins and led astray by various passions,<sup>7</sup>always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth.<sup>8</sup>Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these men also oppose the truth, men corrupted in mind and disqualified regarding the faith.<sup>9</sup>But they will not get very far, for their folly will be plain to all, as was that of those two men.<sup>10</sup>You, however, have followed my teaching, my conduct, my aim in life, my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness,<sup>11</sup>my persecutions and sufferings that happened to me at Antioch, at Iconium, and at Lystra—which persecutions I endured; yet from them all the Lord rescued me.<sup>12</sup>Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted,<sup>13</sup>while evil people and impostors will go on from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived.<sup>14</sup>But as for you, continue in what you have learned and have firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it<sup>15</sup>and how from childhood you have been acquainted with the sacred writings, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus.<sup>16</sup>All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness,<sup>17</sup>that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.

keyVerse.quote: All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, that the man of God may be complete, equipped for every good work.
keyVerse.note: The chapter describes fierce times, convincing imitators and deceivers going from bad to worse; these two verses are what God puts into Timothy’s hand against all of it. Because Scripture comes from God’s own mouth it carries his authority, and because it is profitable for every part of life it is enough: the man of God needs no secret knowledge or new technique, only the book that leads him to Christ.

3.reflection:
Paul’s list in verses 2–5 begins with “lovers of self” and ends with “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God”. Which items on the list are most often treated as normal around you, and which do you recognise in yourself? How does the gospel deal with love turned inward?

Verse 5 describes people with “the appearance of godliness” but not its power. What does the real power of godliness look like in an ordinary Christian life, and how can a church guard against keeping the outline of religion without its reality?

Timothy learned the faith from Paul’s life and from Lois and Eunice (vv. 10–11, 14–15). Who has shaped your faith in this way, and who might be watching you? What could you do to pass the Scriptures on to the next generation?

Verses 16–17 say that all Scripture is breathed out by God and enough to equip us for every good work. Which parts of the Bible do you tend to neglect, and what would it look like this week for Scripture to teach, reprove, correct and train you?

4.title: Preach the Word: The Commission, the Crown, and the Cloak
4.overview:
Where we are. This is the last chapter of Paul’s last letter, and so the last words we have from him. Chapter 3 ended with the Scriptures that are “breathed out by God” and make the man of God complete (3:16–17); chapter 4 turns that into a solemn charge, and then Paul lays down his own work and says goodbye.

The message. Preach the word, because the Judge is coming and people will soon prefer teachers who tell them what they want to hear; and do not fear what faithfulness costs, because the Lord who stood by Paul when everyone left will bring his servants safely home. This is not a hero’s farewell but a servant’s handover: the race was finished by grace, the crown waits for all who love Christ’s appearing, and the last word is grace.

Why it was said. Paul is in a Roman prison, has already faced a first hearing alone, and expects to be executed (see the introduction). Timothy, young and inclined to timidity, is left in Ephesus with false teachers and a gospel that has become dangerous to own. He needs to know what matters most now that his father in the faith is going, and that he will not be left alone.

How the chapter makes its case. First the charge, sworn before Christ the coming Judge: preach the word in every season, with patience (vv. 1–2), because people will heap up teachers to scratch their itching ears (vv. 3–4); so keep your head, endure, evangelise and finish your ministry (v. 5). Then the reason it falls to Timothy now: Paul is being poured out like a drink offering; he has fought, finished and kept, and a crown is laid up for him and for all who love Christ’s appearing (vv. 6–8). The second half is among the most human passages Paul wrote (vv. 9–22): friends gone and one friend staying, a failed man restored, a cloak and books sent for, an enemy handed over to the Lord, a hearing where everyone left but the Lord stood by him, and a short list of people who stayed.

Where it leads. Every part of the chapter rests on Christ. The Judge Timothy must answer to is the one who was judged in our place. The crown of righteousness is given by the righteous Judge, from his own righteousness. And when no one stood by Paul, “the Lord stood by me and strengthened me” (v. 17): the one whose friends deserted him in Gethsemane stood beside his servant in a Roman court, and will bring him through death “safely into his heavenly kingdom” (v. 18). The last word Paul wrote is “grace”.

For us. Ask what you want from preaching: the truth, or the scratch. Ask whether you love Christ’s appearing or this present world. And if you are facing something alone, a hearing, a diagnosis, a loss, take Paul’s words as your own: the Lord stands by his people, and he will bring them safely home.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — Preach the Word, and Finish the Race
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Preach the word in every season, because the Judge is coming and people will soon prefer teachers who please them; Paul’s race is run, and the work passes to Timothy. Paul puts Timothy on oath before Christ the Judge and charges him to preach, correct and encourage with patience (vv. 1–2). The reason is urgent: people will lose their appetite for sound teaching and gather teachers to suit their passions (vv. 3–4). So Timothy must keep his head, endure, evangelise and finish his ministry (v. 5), for Paul is being poured out (v. 6). He has fought, finished and kept the faith, and a crown waits, not only for him but for all who have loved Christ’s appearing (vv. 7–8).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Last Charge, and the Steward's Report

Paul swears Timothy before the court that will judge both him and Nero (v. 1), and his ‘I have kept the faith’ (v. 7) is a steward's report, not a boast (see the note on v. 7). The crown is for all who have loved Christ's appearing (v. 8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The itch is in the hearers' ears (see the note on vv. 3–4).

Now: When did one of your teachers last tell you something you did not want to hear?

verseByVerse.quote: I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who is to judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and exhort, with complete patience and teaching.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Because Christ is coming to judge, Timothy must preach God’s word in every season, correcting and encouraging with patience. Paul’s last charge is sworn before the highest court there is.

I charge you in the presence of God. Few charges in Paul’s letters are more solemn: a court-like oath (compare 1 Timothy 5:21). About to be judged by a Roman court, Paul puts Timothy on oath before a higher one, the God from whose sight no creature is hidden (Hebrews 4:13). Timothy will preach, and every hearer will listen, under that gaze.

Who is to judge the living and the dead. Christ will judge everyone, those alive at his return and those who have died (Acts 10:42; 17:31), as the church has confessed in the creed ever since. Both Paul and Nero will stand before this court, and ministers will give account (Hebrews 13:17).

And by his appearing and his kingdom. His visible return (1 Timothy 6:14) and his rule fully revealed: Timothy is to work in Ephesus with that day in view.

Preach the word. Then the charge, in short commands like hammer blows: five here, four more in verse 5. “Preach” is the herald’s verb: a herald delivers his message; he does not compose or improve it. And its object is the word, the Scriptures just described (3:15–17), not the preacher’s opinions or stories.

Be ready in season and out of season. Literally “well-timed, ill-timed”: when the word is welcome and when it is not. Paul expects plenty of unwelcome times; unpopularity must not silence the word, though this is no licence for tactlessness in personal conversation.

Reprove, rebuke, and exhort. “Reprove” is to show a man he is wrong (3:16); “rebuke” is the sharper warning to stop; “exhort” is to come alongside and encourage. Two are hard and one is warm. A ministry with only the first two beats people down; one with only the third comforts them and never tells them the truth they need.

With complete patience and teaching. Patience, because people change slowly; teaching, because reproof without instruction leaves a man knowing he is wrong and not knowing what is right.

The patience of the Judge. The Judge is coming, and the preacher must be patient, because the Judge himself is patient now. Christ Jesus showed Paul, the foremost of sinners, his “perfect patience” (1 Timothy 1:16), the same word, makrothymia, as here, and he delays the day because he is not wishing that any should perish (2 Peter 3:9). A preacher patient with slow hearers shows them Christ’s own patience while the door of mercy is still open.

The Judge who was judged. The Judge of the living and the dead is the Jesus who was judged in our place. Pilate sat on the bench and the Son of God stood in the dock; one day the positions will be reversed for ever.

What is the difference between preaching the word and giving a good talk? A good talk may be interesting, helpful and even true, and still not be preaching the word. Preaching the word means the message comes out of the text of Scripture and is governed by it: the preacher explains what the passage says, shows how it points to Christ, and presses it on the hearers as God’s own message. The authority is in the word, not the speaker’s personality or opinions; illustrations, warmth and clarity are good servants. The test: after the sermon, do you know better what God has said, and see Christ more clearly?

I sit in the pew, not the pulpit. What does this charge mean for me? Look for a church where the word is preached faithfully, reproof and rebuke as well as comfort. Pray for your pastor, that he will not soften the message to please. Listen as one who will also give account: come prepared, open your Bible, receive correction without resentment, and act on what you hear. And be ready yourself to speak a word from Scripture when it is needed, gently and patiently.

verseByVerse.quote: For the time is coming when people will not endure sound teaching, but having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge is urgent because people will lose their appetite for the truth and collect teachers who tell them what they want to hear. The danger Paul foresees is not so much attack on the truth as boredom with it.

People will not endure sound teaching. “Sound” is the medical word again: the diet that keeps a body well. Sound teaching confronts sin and pride, and people will refuse to tolerate it. The time was already arriving: the myths of verse 4 are the ones these letters resist at Ephesus (1 Timothy 1:4; 4:7), as the last days of 3:1 had already begun.

But having itching ears. Literally having the hearing tickled: ears that want something pleasant, new, flattering, entertaining. And the itch is in the hearers, not the teachers. We generally blame bad teachers for bad churches; Paul says the demand comes first, and teachers appear to supply it. Underneath is a heart that wants God’s blessing without God’s rule, and a God who serves its comfort and success. Today anyone can assemble a set of teachers who agree with him more easily than ever, and believe all the while that he is being discerning.

They will accumulate teachers. To accumulate is to heap up, and they choose by what suits their own desires. They were not misled by a teacher who arrived; they went out and assembled a collection.

And wander off into myths. Whoever stops listening to the truth does not become neutral; there is always something to drift into (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

The teacher the crowds left. Jesus knew what it was for people to stop enduring sound words. When he told the crowd that they must feed on him, the bread of life, many said, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?” and turned back (John 6:60, 66). They had wanted a Messiah who would fill their stomachs and leave their hearts alone (John 6:26). The answer to this verse is Peter’s: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life” (John 6:68). The truth people turn from is finally not a system but a person, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

God loves us too much to scratch our ears. He tells us the truth about our sin, because only the truth leads to the Saviour. The myths of men promise much and deliver nothing; the gospel promises everything and has delivered it in a crucified and risen Christ.

What it does not mean. Not that a popular preacher must be unfaithful, or an unpopular one faithful. The test is faithfulness to the word.

Is it wrong to listen to preachers online, beyond my own church? Not in itself. Good preaching online and in books has fed many believers, especially the housebound and those with no faithful church nearby. The danger is the one Paul names: sampling until you find voices that confirm what you already want. Online listening should supplement, never replace, belonging to a local church, where elders who watch for your soul know and correct you (Hebrews 13:17). Choose a few sound teachers rather than many, and notice whether any of them ever unsettles you. If none does, the selection may be yours and not God’s.

What if the preaching in my church is weak, though faithful? Be patient, and be a help. Plain preaching that explains Scripture accurately and points to Christ is far better than gifted preaching that drifts from the word. Pray for your pastor, encourage him specifically, and come hungry; much depends on the ears as well as the mouth. If the preaching has actually departed from the gospel, it may be right to look for a faithful church (2:20–21). But to leave a faithful church for a more entertaining one is precisely the itch this verse describes.

verseByVerse.quote: As for you, always be sober-minded, endure suffering, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whatever others do, Timothy must keep his head, bear the cost, keep announcing the gospel and finish the work God has given him. Four short commands answer the itching ears of verses 3–4.

As for you, always be sober-minded. “As for you” is the contrast that runs through these letters (3:10, 14). “Be sober-minded” means clear-headed, literally “not drunk”: in a church heaping up teachers, Timothy is to keep his head (1 Thessalonians 5:6). It is not a glamorous instruction, and it comes first.

What a sober mind looks like. A drunk man is not necessarily unhappy; he simply cannot see straight, and is carried along by whatever is in front of him. A sober-minded Christian is not carried away by the mood of the moment. He checks his convictions against Scripture, not against what everyone is saying this week; he does not panic at the news or get swept up by a new teacher; he knows his weak points and does not drift towards them; he keeps enough quiet in his week to think and pray; and he keeps the end in view, because nothing clears the head like knowing where history is going.

Endure suffering. The same root as “share in suffering” (1:8; 2:3); the strength comes from the spirit of power God has given (1:7–8).

Do the work of an evangelist. An evangelist is a bringer of good news; the word occurs only three times in the New Testament (here; Acts 21:8, of Philip; Ephesians 4:11). Timothy’s work in Ephesus was largely corrective, and such a man could spend his whole ministry on maintenance. Paul tells him to keep announcing the good news to people who have not heard it. It is a work, a task to be done, not only a gift some possess: pastoral work and evangelism belong together.

Fulfill your ministry. Carry it out completely (Colossians 4:17). Paul has finished his course (v. 7); Timothy must finish his. And it is your ministry: Timothy is not asked to be a second Paul.

The good news has a name. The good news is a person: Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, the offspring of David (2:8). The suffering Timothy must endure follows the road of that gospel, for his Lord went through the cross to the crown (2:12); Timothy is asked not to suffer for a cause but to share the road of the one he announces. Peter ties a sober mind to the same hope: “set your hope fully on the grace that will be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 1:13). And behind every finished ministry stands the Lord who said on the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30): because he finished his work, his servants can be faithful in theirs, small as they are.

Is evangelist an office today, and must every Christian evangelise? Christ gives evangelists to the church (Ephesians 4:11), and the church still sends people to preach the gospel where it is not known. Timothy, as a pastor, was to do the evangelist’s work. Every believer is to be ready to speak of Christ (1 Peter 3:15), though not all are gifted as evangelists.

What is my ministry, if I am not a pastor? The service God has given you where he has put you: your gifts (1 Peter 4:10), the people around you, and the opportunities that open in front of you. A mother raising children in the Lord, an elderly widow who prays, a teenager inviting a friend to church, a deacon who visits the sick: each has a ministry to fulfil. Do not compare yours with anyone else’s. Ask what the Lord has given you to do, and do it to the end.

In everyday life. Pray for an opportunity to share the gospel with one person you know this week, and be ready with a short, clear account of what Christ has done.

verseByVerse.quote: For I am already being poured out as a drink offering, and the time of my departure has come.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s death is near, and he sees it not as Rome disposing of a prisoner but as his life’s last offering to God and a setting sail. That is why Timothy must now carry on the work.

Already being poured out. “Poured out as a drink offering” is one word, spendomai: the wine poured out with a sacrifice, completing it (Numbers 15:1–10). From an earlier prison Paul spoke of this as something that might happen (“Even if I am to be poured out”, Philippians 2:17). Now there is no “if”: the pouring has already begun.

And the time of my departure has come. “Departure” (analysis; compare Philippians 1:23) is a loosing: the related verb was used of untying a ship from the quay, striking a tent, freeing a prisoner from his chains. Paul chooses a word of release for his own execution.

Priest, not victim. Rome thinks it is getting rid of a troublesome prisoner; Paul says he is being offered to God. There is neither panic nor resignation in the sentence: a man weeks or months from execution reaches for the language of the altar and of a boat casting off, and in the next breath asks for his coat.

The sacrifice behind the drink offering. A drink offering was never the sacrifice itself; it was poured beside one. Paul does not name the sacrifice here (in Philippians 2:17 it was his converts’ faith), but every Christian offering rests on one that came first. The Servant poured out his soul to death and bore the sin of many (Isaiah 53:12), and Jesus called the cup his blood of the covenant, poured out for many (Mark 14:24). Christ’s offering, the full payment for sin, needed nothing added. Paul’s death is the small drink offering of a grateful servant, the last act of a life offered as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1). So our deaths pay for nothing; they are a homecoming: the mooring rope is untied, the tent is struck, and the soul sets sail for the harbour where Christ is.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul’s death atones for sin. Christ’s sacrifice alone does that (Hebrews 10:14). Paul’s death is an offering of thanksgiving and devotion.

What happens to a believer at the moment of death? The soul goes at once to be with Christ (Luke 23:43; 2 Corinthians 5:8), with no soul sleep and no purgatory, while the body rests until the resurrection: hence Paul’s word for setting sail.

How can a Christian face death without fear? Not by pretending it is nothing; death is an enemy (1 Corinthians 15:26), and its weight is natural to feel. But Christ has drawn its sting by bearing our sin, and death can no longer condemn us (1 Corinthians 15:55–57); for the believer it is a departure to be with Christ, which is far better. Many who feared death for years have found grace when the hour came; God gives strength for the day, not before it. Prepare by living close to Christ now, setting your affairs in order, and speaking to your family about your hope. It is not wrong to want to live longer for others’ sake (Philippians 1:24). It is a gift to be able to go in peace.

In everyday life. If you knew your own departure were near, what would you want to say to the people you love? Say one of those things this week.
verseByVerse.note: A drink offering of wine was poured out over a sacrifice.

verseByVerse.quote: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
verseByVerse.commentary:
At the end of his life Paul can say that, by God’s grace, he stayed in the fight, ran to the finish and guarded the gospel unchanged. Three short sentences sum up a whole life.

I have fought the good fight. Each clause uses a Greek tense for a finished act whose result still stands. It is the charge he gave Timothy (1 Timothy 6:12), now reported of himself. He does not say he won every engagement, only that the contest was worth entering and he stayed in it to the end.

I have finished the race. Years earlier, at Miletus, Paul told the Ephesian elders he only wanted to finish his course (Acts 20:24). He wanted one thing for years, and at the end he can say he has done it.

I have kept the faith. To keep is to guard. He has kept faith with Christ, as one keeps a promise; and he has kept the faith, the gospel entrusted to him (“the good deposit”, 1:14), unchanged. This letter has pressed so hard on guarding that deposit that the second is surely the main meaning.

A steward’s report. The man who wrote that grace was given not because of works (1:9), and who called himself the foremost of sinners, is not congratulating himself. This is a servant telling his master that the task is done. Most people reach the end with things unfinished, unsure what their life was for; Paul can say it because his life had one aim (3:10).

The keeper behind the keeping. He could keep the faith because he was kept: “he is able to guard until that day what has been entrusted to me” (1:12). The man who says “I have kept” has been held, through floggings, shipwreck and prison, by a Saviour from whose hand no one can snatch his sheep (John 10:28).

A perfect race counted to us. One man fought the fight, finished the race and kept the faith perfectly, enduring the cross for the joy set before him (Hebrews 12:2), and he did it for us. Our running is never flawless, but his perfect race is counted to everyone who trusts him, and he stands at the end of ours holding the crown. The grace that carried Paul from the Damascus road to the Ostian road outside Rome, where tradition says he was beheaded, carries the weakest Christian home.

The résumé and the eulogy. The writer David Brooks has distinguished résumé virtues, the skills and successes you bring to the market, from eulogy virtues, the things said at your funeral: whether you were kind, brave, honest, faithful. Look at Paul’s résumé on the day he wrote this: in chains, Asia turned away, Demas gone, false teachers troubling his churches. By the usual measures, failure. Yet all three of his sentences are about faithfulness, not results, and he is at peace. That overturns both the achiever, who must leave an impressive record, and the drifter, who thinks nothing is at stake. And it guards against making faithfulness itself a résumé to wave at God: the crown is “of righteousness”, given by a judge who counts Christ’s finished race to his people (v. 8). A life is finally measured not by what it built but by whom it loved.

I have failed so often. Could I ever say these words? Yes, if you mean what Paul meant. He was not claiming a flawless record; he had been a persecutor, and he wrote openly of his struggle with sin (Romans 7:15–25). He meant that by grace he had not given up or let go of Christ and the gospel. Every true believer will be able to say the same, because God keeps them (Philippians 1:6; 1 Peter 1:5). The fight includes many falls and many restorations. What matters is that you are still in it when the bell rings, and that is his gift.

What does keeping the faith look like for an ordinary Christian? Holding on to the gospel you received rather than exchanging it for something more fashionable, and handing it on unchanged. And keeping faith with Christ: staying loyal to him through suffering, temptation and long dull years; going on praying, gathering with his people, confessing sin and trusting his promises. A grandmother who believed and taught the Scriptures for sixty years has kept the faith as truly as an apostle.

In everyday life. Most of the race is run on ordinary days: getting up to pray when tired, saying no to the same temptation again. None of it feels like a good fight, but that is what the fight mostly is.

verseByVerse.quote: Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award to me on that day, and not only to me but also to all who have loved his appearing.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A crown of righteousness is waiting for Paul, and the righteous Judge will give the same crown to everyone who longs for Christ’s return. The unjust verdict of Rome will not be the last word.

Henceforth there is laid up for me. “Laid up” means reserved, put by for someone: already there, waiting, with his name on it (Colossians 1:5; 1 Peter 1:4).

The crown of righteousness. The crown is the victor’s wreath at the games (2:5), not a king’s crown: the picture of the athlete carried to its end. The prize is being finally and fully right with God, which Paul spent his life insisting could not be earned: vindication, being declared in the right in public, as Christ was vindicated when God raised him (1 Timothy 3:16). This is justification made public. God pronounces the believing sinner righteous, his own record set aside and Christ’s obedience and death reckoned to his account (Romans 4:5; 5:1); that verdict is given the moment a person believes, and on that day it will be announced before the whole creation. The other crowns of the New Testament, of life (James 1:12), of glory (1 Peter 5:4), imperishable (1 Corinthians 9:25), describe the one reward of eternal life with Christ.

Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will award. Paul awaits the verdict of a Roman court he expects to find against him, and looks past it to a judge who is righteous, as the one in Rome is not. Here is comfort for anyone treated unjustly who can do nothing about it: Paul does not minimise the injustice; he appeals it to a higher court, and waits. And the Judge who hands out the crown is the one who wore the thorns, so that the righteousness he crowns us with is his own.

But also to all who have loved his appearing. This clause opens the promise to every believer. The crown is not a special award for apostles or martyrs but for all who long for Christ to come. It is a fair test of where our treasure is: a man tells you what he loves by what he hopes is coming.

What it does not mean. It does not mean Paul earned salvation by his works. The crown is a gracious reward. As Augustine said, when God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts.

I do not long for Christ’s return. Sometimes I dread it. Ask why. If it is because you love this world more than him, heed the warning (Demas deserted Paul for love of this present world, v. 10), and ask Christ to change your loves. But many dread it for other reasons: fear of judgment, confusion about what will happen, or a good life they cannot imagine bettering. Then let Scripture fill your imagination. For those in Christ his appearing means no condemnation, the end of sin and grief, the resurrection of the body, reunion with believing loved ones, and the face of the one who loved you. The more you know him, the more you will want him to come.

Is it wrong to be motivated by reward? No, if the reward is rightly understood. Jesus motivates his disciples with reward (Matthew 6:19–21; 5:12), and Moses looked to it (Hebrews 11:26). It is not wages earned but a gift of grace, and at its heart it is Christ himself; wanting that is not mercenary but what love wants. What would be wrong is serving to put God in our debt. Faithful service will be acknowledged on that day (1 Corinthians 3:12–14), yet every crown will be cast before the throne, because every crown was his gift.

In everyday life. This week, end your prayers with the last prayer of the Bible: “Come, Lord Jesus!” (Revelation 22:20). Notice what in your life makes it hard to pray that honestly, and bring that to him too.

Uncertain wording. “The crown of righteousness” may mean a crown that is righteousness, a crown rewarding a righteous life, or a crown from the righteous Judge; the Greek allows each. The first fits Paul best, as explained above.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When friends fail, the Lord stands by his servant and brings him safely home, and so Paul’s last word is grace. He asks Timothy to come quickly, because Demas has deserted him for love of this present world, others are away and only Luke remains; Mark, once a failure, is sent for as very useful (vv. 9–12). He wants his cloak and his books (v. 13). He leaves Alexander’s harm to the Lord, yet warns Timothy about him (vv. 14–15). At his first defence all deserted him, and he prays that it not be charged against them; but the Lord stood by him and will bring him into his heavenly kingdom (vv. 16–18). Greetings, a sick friend left behind, a plea to come before winter, and grace close the letter (vv. 19–22).
verseByVerse.theology:
Two Kinds of Wrong, Two Different Prayers

Of Alexander Paul says only that the Lord will repay (v. 14); of the friends who deserted him he prays ‘may it not be charged against them’ (v. 16). It is Stephen's prayer (see the note on vv. 16–18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Demas left for love of this present world; Mark, once refused, is sent for as ‘very useful’ (vv. 10–11).

Now: Five verses after the crown of righteousness, Paul asks for his cloak and his books (see the note on v. 13).

verseByVerse.quote: Do your best to come to me soon. For Demas, in love with this present world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Luke alone is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is very useful to me for ministry. Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul is nearly alone: one friend has left him for love of this world, others are away on the Lord’s work, and he sends for the man he once refused. The great apostle asks his young friend to hurry.

Do your best to come to me soon. After the crown and the righteous judge, the apostle asks a young man to come quickly. He is lonely, and his time is short.

For Demas has deserted me. We met Demas sending greetings alongside Luke (Colossians 4:14; Philemon 24): a fellow worker. The charge is not heresy or scandal: he loved this present age, the deliberate opposite of loving Christ’s appearing (v. 8). That is how most people leave: not by renouncing Christ but by preferring something else. Something ordinary and legitimate, comfort, safety, a quieter life, became more attractive than a chained old man in Rome. Nobody would have accused Demas of anything at the time.

Crescens has gone to Galatia, Titus to Dalmatia. Galatia is probably the region in central Turkey (see the textual note below); Dalmatia is on the Adriatic coast, so Titus, once left on Crete (Titus 1:5; 3:12), has moved on to work further north. No blame attaches to these two; they have gone on ministry. But the room is empty either way.

Luke alone is with me. Luke, the beloved physician, who shared the shipwreck and wrote its story, is still there when everyone else has gone.

Get Mark and bring him. The sentence is lovely for what it does not say. John Mark had abandoned Paul and Barnabas mid-journey (Acts 13:13), and Paul had refused to take him again, so sharply that he and Barnabas parted (Acts 15:37–40). Now, at the end of everything, Paul sends for him and calls him “very useful”, the word he used of Onesimus, another man who had failed (Philemon 11). There is no defensiveness and no revisiting of the old argument, and the church has received from Mark, as early tradition holds, the Gospel that bears his name. Grace restores the failed, and it also restores the people who gave up on them.

Tychicus I have sent to Ephesus. A trusted messenger (Ephesians 6:21), perhaps carrying this letter and replacing Timothy while he travelled. Even alone in a cell, Paul is arranging for the churches to be cared for.

The age Christ died to rescue us from. “This present world” is literally “the now age”, and Christ “gave himself for our sins to deliver us from the present evil age” (Galatians 1:4). Demas fell in love with the very order of things from which his Lord had died to set him free. So the two loves of verses 8 and 10 cannot share one heart: to love Christ’s appearing is to long for the age he will bring; to love the now age is, in the end, to prefer that he stay away.

The friend who never deserts. The Lord who restored Mark restored Peter, and every one of us; he turns deserters into Gospel writers. And he never deserts: when the room empties, he remains, the friend who sticks closer than a brother.

Did Demas lose his salvation, or was he never saved? Scripture does not tell us his end. If he never returned, the Reformed reading is that he showed he had never truly belonged (1 John 2:19); Arminian Christians (who hold that a true believer can finally fall away) would read him as a believer who did. He may have repented. Either way, his story warns us to love Christ’s appearing more than this present world.

What does loving this present world look like now? Rarely wild sin. It looks like Demas: a quiet preference for comfort, safety and success over Christ and his people. Taking the promotion that moves you away from any faithful church without a second thought; drifting from fellowship because Sundays are full; avoiding a suffering friend; deciding that wholehearted discipleship can wait until life is less busy. The world here is not creation or people, whom God loves, but the present age organised without God (1 John 2:15–17). The test is what you would give up for Christ, and what you are giving up Christ for.

Someone failed me badly, or I failed someone. Can it really be restored? Mark is God’s answer that it can. Restoration needs repentance from the one who failed, which Mark showed over years of faithful service, and readiness in the one wronged to see God’s grace at work and say so. It does not mean pretending the failure did not happen, or rushing trust before it is earned, but it does mean refusing to define a brother for ever by his worst moment. If you failed, keep serving faithfully; God can make you useful again. If you were wronged, look for the signs of change, and be willing to send for Mark.

In everyday life. Every church has someone lonely in the faith: the elderly, the imprisoned, the missionary far from home. A Luke is simply a person who stays.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read “Gaul” instead of “Galatia” in verse 10. The difference is smaller than it looks, since Greek writers could call Gaul “Galatia” too; either way, Crescens had gone on the Lord’s work.
verseByVerse.note: Mark, who had once deserted Paul, is now “very useful.” Dalmatia lay on the Adriatic coast.

verseByVerse.quote: When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, also the books, and above all the parchments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A man about to die asks for a warm coat and something to read: faith does not float above the body’s needs, and Paul is still learning to the end.

Bring the cloak. Five verses after the crown of righteousness, the same man thinks about eternity and about being cold. The cloak was a heavy woollen cape, the kind a poor man might own only one of; Paul may have been arrested at Troas suddenly and left his things. A Roman prison in winter is a serious matter for a man no longer young (v. 21).

Also the books, and above all the parchments. The books were scrolls; the parchments, of animal skin, were more durable and costly (see the box below). A man weeks or months from execution sends across the empire for something to read: he is still learning to the end.

Tyndale’s echo. William Tyndale, imprisoned at Vilvoorde in the winter before his execution, wrote asking for a warmer cap, a woollen shirt, and above all his Hebrew Bible, grammar and dictionary: one prisoner understood another exactly.

A Lord who knew the cold. Paul’s request is not beneath the gospel, because the gospel is about a Son who took a real body (John 1:14): he grew tired at a well (John 4:6), had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20), and on the cross said, “I thirst” (John 19:28). Our high priest is able to sympathise with our weaknesses (Hebrews 4:15), including a body shivering in a cell. The God who numbers the hairs of our heads knows when his servants are cold, and he will raise the cold, worn body of his servant in glory.

Is it unspiritual to ask for practical help? Not at all. Paul asks plainly for a coat, as he thanked Onesiphorus for practical refreshment (1:16) and the Philippians for money (Philippians 4:14–18). Pride sometimes dresses itself as spirituality and refuses to admit need; humility asks. God usually meets our needs through his people (Galatians 6:2). Pray and trust him; then tell a brother or sister what you need.

Should Christians read widely, or only the Bible? Paul wanted his books, and above all the parchments: the right order. Scripture comes first and governs everything else, but other good reading, theology, history, biography, literature, can feed the mind and serve faith; Paul quoted Greek poets (Acts 17:28). Read with discernment, and keep learning as long as you live.

In everyday life. Somewhere this winter a believer is cold, or short of something to read. A coat, a book or a letter is no small thing to the one who receives it; Paul thought them worth a sentence of Scripture.

Uncertain wording. Paul does not say what the parchments held. Most likely portions of the Old Testament, which fits “above all”; others suggest his own notebooks or legal papers.
verseByVerse.note: With winter coming (v. 21), Paul wants his heavy cloak; the parchments may have been copies of Scripture.

verseByVerse.quote: Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. Beware of him yourself, for he strongly opposed our message.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul names the harm Alexander did him, leaves the repaying to the Lord, and still warns Timothy to be on his guard. Forgiveness and protection stand side by side.

Alexander the coppersmith. Possibly the Alexander of 1 Timothy 1:20, though the name was common. We are told only that he “did me great harm”; perhaps he informed against Paul.

The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. Paul has been badly injured and does not pretend otherwise, or produce a strained forgiveness that denies the damage. But he does not retaliate; he hands the matter to the Lord, as he taught (Romans 12:19). A Christian can let an injury go not because it did not matter but because someone better placed will deal with it.

Beware of him yourself. His opposition was to the gospel, not merely to Paul. Forgiveness never required anybody to be naive, and warning a colleague about a dangerous person is not gossip but protection.

The same hands crown and repay. The Lord who will repay Alexander is the righteous judge of verse 8: one Greek verb lies behind “award” there and “repay” here, and the hands are the same. Paul learned this letting go from Christ, who, when he was reviled, did not revile in return, but kept entrusting himself to him who judges justly (1 Peter 2:23).

Not one injury overlooked. Not one injury done to his people will be overlooked, and not one punished twice: either it was borne by Christ at the cross for those who repent, or it will be answered in full on the last day. And the man who wrote this verse once did great harm to the church himself, and the Lord he persecuted made him an apostle (1 Timothy 1:13).

Is it wrong to want justice for what someone did to me? No. Wanting wrong put right is part of bearing the image of a just God, and the psalms are full of cries for justice. What is forbidden is taking vengeance yourself, or nursing hatred. Name the harm truthfully, refuse revenge, hand the case to the Lord, and keep praying, even for your enemy’s repentance (Matthew 5:44). God has also given authorities to punish wrongdoing (Romans 13:4), so reporting a crime or abuse is not unforgiving: you can forgive from the heart and still let the courts do their work.

How do I forgive someone and still warn others about them? By keeping two duties distinct. Forgiveness releases your claim to pay them back and wishes them good, including repentance. Protection tells the truth where others are at risk. Paul did both in two verses. If a person has abused, defrauded or deceived, you may and sometimes must warn those who could be harmed, report it to the proper authorities, and keep appropriate distance. Abuse is never to be covered up in the name of forgiveness. Avoid only spreading the story further than protection requires, or speaking with relish. Warn as Paul did: briefly, factually, for the sake of others.

Textual note. Some manuscripts read a wish, “may the Lord repay him”, but the better reading is a plain statement: Paul is not calling down harm but leaving the case with the Lord.

parallels.desc: you will render to a man according to his work

verseByVerse.quote: At my first defense no one came to stand by me, but all deserted me. May it not be charged against them! But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message might be fully proclaimed and all the Gentiles might hear it. So I was rescued from the lion's mouth. The Lord will rescue me from every evil deed and bring me safely into his heavenly kingdom. To him be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
verseByVerse.commentary:
When every friend failed Paul at his hearing, the Lord stood beside him and used the moment to proclaim the gospel, and he will carry Paul through death into his kingdom.

No one came to stand by me. A legal phrase. At a hearing a defendant would ordinarily have friends to speak for his character or act as advocates. Paul had none; “deserted” is the word used of Demas (v. 10).

May it not be charged against them! It is Stephen’s prayer as the stones struck him: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:60), and Paul had stood there approving (Acts 8:1). Some thirty years later, deserted himself, he prays what he once watched a dying man pray, and what his Lord prayed on the cross (Luke 23:34; a verse missing from some early manuscripts of Luke, though widely held to be genuine). He does not excuse them; it was a sin. They were weak and afraid, not malicious like Alexander, and he asks that it not be charged.

But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me. No one came to stand by him, and then the Lord did: the support Paul was owed and did not get was supplied by someone else, in the same room, at the same hour (Acts 23:11; Hebrews 13:5). That is the whole comfort of the passage.

That all the Gentiles might hear it. Typically, Paul’s concern is not his acquittal but the message: his defence became a sermon in the capital of the Gentile world.

So I was rescued from the lion’s mouth. A proverbial expression for mortal danger (Psalm 22:21; Daniel 6:20–22). The hearing did not end in a death sentence: he lived to write this letter.

From every evil deed. The words echo the Lord’s Prayer, “deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13). But Paul knows he will die (v. 6); he expects to be brought through the execution safely into the kingdom. That is Christian confidence at close range: not that nothing bad will happen, but that nothing bad can stop him arriving. And so comes his last doxology.

In the flow. These verses gather up the letter: the desertion of Asia (1:15) repeated in a courtroom, the strength Timothy was told to draw on (2:1), the word unbound while the apostle is chained (2:9), the confidence of 1:12 spoken at the edge of death.

He was deserted before we were. In Gethsemane his friends slept; at the cross he cried that his God had forsaken him. He stood alone so that no believer need ever stand alone, and now he stands beside his servants in every courtroom, every hospital, every lonely room. To him be the glory for ever and ever. Amen.

I have felt abandoned, and I did not feel the Lord standing by me. What then? Many believers have known that darkness, and Scripture does not hide it (Psalm 88; Psalm 22:1). Feelings are not the measure of his presence. He has promised never to leave you nor forsake you (Hebrews 13:5), and he kept it when you could not sense it, which is why you are still holding on. Tell him honestly how it feels, as the psalmists did, and watch in the Gospels how he treats the lonely. And go to his people, because one way he stands by us is by sending an Onesiphorus, who searched Rome for Paul until he found him (1:16–17), or a Luke, who stayed (v. 11).

How do I pray for people who failed me when I needed them? As Paul did: may it not be charged against them. That does not say it did not matter; it asks God to forgive them as he has forgiven you. Name the failure honestly, admit the hurt, and deliberately ask for their good. You may need to pray it many times before your heart agrees with your words. In time it may be right to speak to them, gently. But first release them into God’s mercy, where you yourself have been standing all along.

In everyday life. If you are facing something alone this week, a hearing, a diagnosis, a hard conversation, ask the Lord beforehand to stand by you. And if you know someone facing their own first defence alone, go and stand with them.

Uncertain wording. The “first defense” is most likely the preliminary hearing of Paul’s present trial; some early writers took it as his earlier trial at the end of Acts, but the desertion and the death he expects fit the present trial better. “The lion’s mouth” is most likely a proverb for mortal danger; some see Nero or the devil (1 Peter 5:8) in it, and a Roman citizen could not lawfully be thrown to real lions.
verseByVerse.note: The “first defense” was a preliminary hearing at his trial.

parallels.desc: Save me from the mouth of the lion

verseByVerse.quote: Greet Prisca and Aquila, and the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus remained at Corinth, and I left Trophimus, who was ill, at Miletus. Do your best to come before winter. Eubulus sends greetings to you, as do Pudens and Linus and Claudia and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul’s last words are greetings to friends, honest news of a colleague left sick, a plea to come before winter, and grace. The letter that records the desertions ends with people who stayed, and with the Lord who stays.

Greet Prisca and Aquila. Prisca and Aquila, the tentmaking couple Paul met in Corinth after their expulsion from Rome, worked with him in Corinth and Ephesus, took Apollos aside to explain the way of God more accurately, and once risked their necks for his life (Acts 18:2–3, 18, 26; Romans 16:3–4). Prisca (Priscilla) is often named first, perhaps for her prominence in ministry or social standing. They were probably back in Ephesus. Paul greets the household of Onesiphorus (1:16–18) rather than the man himself, which many take to mean he had since died.

I left Trophimus, who was ill. Erastus is possibly the city treasurer of Corinth (Romans 16:23); Trophimus was a Gentile from Ephesus who travelled with Paul (Acts 20:4). Paul probably names them to explain why two familiar co-workers are not with him. The note about Trophimus is quietly significant: Paul, through whom God did extraordinary miracles (Acts 19:11–12), did not heal him. The apostles could not heal whoever they chose, whenever they chose.

Do your best to come before winter. Winter closed the Mediterranean to shipping from about November to March; if Timothy waited, he might arrive too late. Behind the instruction is a man counting weeks. We do not know whether Timothy made it.

Eubulus sends greetings. Four names we meet nowhere else in Scripture: Roman believers keeping company with a condemned man when Demas would not (Irenaeus names Linus as the first leader of the church at Rome after the apostles). This does not contradict “Luke alone is with me” (v. 11): there Paul means the companions who travelled and worked with him; these were members of the Roman church who could still visit or send word.

The Lord be with your spirit. The last sentence of Paul’s that we possess. The first half is singular: “your” is Timothy, the young man told to fan God’s gift into flame (1:6). Paul may never see him again, so he commits him to the one companion who cannot be taken. The Lord who stood by Paul (v. 17) is asked now to stand by Timothy, as the risen Christ promised all his servants: “I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20). Apostles die; the Lord of the apostles stays with his church.

Grace be with you. The second half is plural: the whole church. The last written word of the apostle to the Gentiles is grace. After the shipwrecks and floggings, the churches and arguments, the deposit guarded and handed on, the desertions and the cloak left at Troas: grace. It is the word on which nearly all his letters close, and the right one. God had the first word too, giving grace in Christ Jesus before the ages began (1:9), and every word between, the calling, the keeping, the strengthening, the rescuing, has been grace.

What it does not mean. Trophimus’s illness does not mean he lacked faith, or that God does not heal today: he still heals in answer to prayer, as he wills (James 5:14–15). But the apostolic sign gifts were not possessions to be used at will, and they ceased with the apostolic era. This commentary holds that cessationist view because Scripture ties the signs to the apostles and the founding of the church (2 Corinthians 12:12; Ephesians 2:20); many faithful Christians believe such gifts continue, and they too pray for the sick in faith.

We prayed for someone to be healed and they were not. Did we fail? No. Paul prayed and Trophimus stayed ill; Paul prayed three times about his own thorn and it stayed (2 Corinthians 12:7–9). God is not a machine that heals when enough faith is inserted. He heals as he wills, sometimes by medicine, sometimes beyond it, sometimes not in this life, and the final healing of every believer is the resurrection. Keep praying; call the elders, and use doctors gratefully. When healing does not come, God is still good and his grace still sufficient. Anyone who tells a sick believer he is ill because his faith is weak has not read this verse.

Why are all these names in the Bible? Because the gospel is carried by people, and God remembers them: named individuals, couples, households, the sick and the faithful, men and women, many of whom we know nothing else about. Paul, for all his greatness, depended on friends. Your name may never be in a book. It is written in a better one (Luke 10:20; Philippians 4:3).

In everyday life. If there is something you need to do before winter, a visit, a reconciliation, a word of thanks to someone who may not be here in spring, do it now.

Where Christians differ: does Linus show papal succession? Roman Catholic tradition lists Linus as the second pope after Peter, as evidence of an unbroken papal succession. This commentary’s view: Paul mentions Linus only as one Roman believer among others, without any title. Early lists name him as a leader of the Roman church, but the New Testament knows nothing of a single bishop ruling the universal church. Churches were led by a plurality of elders. Christ alone is head of the church (Ephesians 1:22; Colossians 1:18), and apostolic succession is succession in apostolic teaching.
verseByVerse.note: Winter closed the Mediterranean to shipping, so Timothy had to sail before it. Paul had healed others, yet left Trophimus ill.

keyVerse.quote: I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith.
keyVerse.note: These three sentences gather up Paul’s whole life and explain the charge of verses 1–5: the work passes to Timothy because Paul’s is done. They are a steward’s report, not a boast, and the next verse shows what they rest on: a crown of righteousness given by the righteous Judge to all who love his appearing. What grace enabled Paul to say, it will enable every believer to say.

4.reflection:
Verses 3–4 put the itch in the hearers’ ears, not in the teachers’ mouths. What do you most want from the preaching you hear? When did a sermon last tell you something you did not want to hear, and how did you respond?

Paul’s three sentences in verse 7 are about faithfulness, not results. How would measuring your life that way change what you are aiming at? What does keeping the faith look like in an ordinary week?

Demas was “in love with this present world” (v. 10); the crown is for “all who have loved his appearing” (v. 8). What quiet preferences compete most with your longing for Christ’s return?

Paul leaves Alexander to the Lord, prays for the friends who failed him, and sends for Mark, whom he once refused (vv. 11, 14–16). Is there someone you need to release, restore or send for? How does “the Lord stood by me” (v. 17) make that possible?
